MR. DIEFENBAKER-REFERENCE TO RETURN RESPECTING CAMP BORDEN ARMY REJECTION OR MEDICAL DISCHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to bring to the attention of the house a breach of the privileges of parliament by reason of the incompleteness and incorrectness of a return brought down yesterday, sessional paper No. 258, which was passed pursuant to an order of the house dated August 7, 1946.
The order in question reads as follows:
A copy of all correspondence passing between the Department of National Defence, and/or the Department of Labour, and/or the Department of Justice, and between any one or more of said departments since January, 1944, to date, in connection with the improper use of army rejection or medical discharges at Camp Borden, wherein one Arnold (also known as William Horrigan), allegedly along with one Bagley utilized army rejection or medical discharges which had been signed in, in blank, by former Major J. A. Elliott, A. 19, R.C.A.S.C.
A perusal of the documents produced yesterday shows that in spite of the fact that parliament passed the order without any qualifications that any documents should be refused, a number of the letters have been deliberately omitted and the file is in the position of having been stripped and denuded of four known letters, as well as others. The four letters which do not appear in the file are the following:
(1)	A letter from Mr. Robinette, K.C., of Toronto, dated March 22, referred to in letter of March 26.
(2)	Letter from Mr. Miall to Mr. Anderson, dated the 26th of March.
(3)	Copy of letter, October 12, from Mr. Robinette, K.C., sent to Mr. MacNamara, the deputy minister.
(4)	Letter of the deputy minister of justice to Mr. MacNamara, dated the 19th of October, 1945.

These four letters are referred to in the correspondence produced, but have not been produced.
In addition to that there is correspondence I know of which shows that the R.C.M.P. found a definite case against Arnold, Elliott and Bagley, and that there was also evidence that the fake medical rejection certificates signed by Elliott at Camp Borden with the name of the recipient left in blank were sold to various persons, one of the recipients claiming that he had paid approximately SI,300 to Bagley.
I say, sir, that when letters in the possession of the department or departments of government are deleted from the record when a return or reply is brought down to this house, it is an affront to parliament and to the privileges of parliament. Parliament is entitled to full information, not to information as selected by government officials, or as to what information government officials consider sufficient for the needs or good of parliament.
This case has odoriferous characteristics. The deletion of a major portion of the record will not down the suspicion that there were reasons why the Royal Canadian Mounted Police report recommending prosecution was departed from on the recommendations of the Deputy Minister of Labour.
What I want to know is this: Where are the rest of the documents, and when will they be produced?
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs):	May I say that the
Minister of National Defence, who has been engaged for two or three hours with treasury board, will be here later to-day, and will reply, effectively, as usual, to the allegations of my hon. friend.

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee on bill No. 345, respecting the construction of a line of railway by Canadian National Railway Company from Barraute to Kiask Falls on the Bell river in the province of Quebec.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Construction and completion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM B.ARRAUTE TO KIASK FALLS, QUEBEC
speechtext:
I want to say a few words about this bill, and I imagine that as a result of what I say the minister will give us some information. I notice in the proceedings of the committee which considered this bill a few days ago that a witness is reported as having said that there are about 75,000 people living in this area. The minister is reported on page 45 to have asked:
Are there not about 75,000 people in that country?
The Witness:	There are about 75,000 in the
country.
I hope that the support given, by this house to this bill is not based on information such as that. The whole riding of Chapleau, which extends for 350 miles from east to west, has only about 45,000 people, or less.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM B.ARRAUTE TO KIASK FALLS, QUEBEC
speechtext: There are many more than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM B.ARRAUTE TO KIASK FALLS, QUEBEC
speechtext:
The 1941 census shows 43,416, so when I said "or less" I was about correct. I do not usually make misstatements.

I am for the bill, and I am not making this statement to oppose it, but I do want to feel certain that the line is going to pay. We have altogether too many branch lines on the Canadian National Railways that are nothing but white elephants.
I notice that the pulpwood from Barraute will have to be taken by freight to Windsor Mills in Quebec, a distance of about 500 miles. Is that not quite a long distance to take pulpwood? I am just wondering whether it would be an investment. I notice in the evidence this statement by a witness: "We know that the soil is excellent." There is no reason why it should not be. It appears to me to be the same type of country as in northern Ontario and should be a good farming country. But it is the next- statement made by the witness that makes me wonder:
There is a rather happy compensating feature which is present. This whole country slopes to the north and the consequence is that as you go north you lower the elevation.
The elevation at Barraute is 1,024 feet above sea level, and at lake Mattagami, a hundred ' miles north, the elevation is 765 feet. That is not much of a slope in 100 miles. I know the minister's task as administrator of this department is an onerous one, but I would suggest that in receiving from the Canadian National Railways applications for branch lines all the particulars pertaining to the country to be run through be studied by him as well as by those who furnish him with reports. I am not opposing the bill. In fact I am all for that country being opened up. But the little information supplied is not a very good foundation on which to base a programme of construction.
I suggest to the minister, although this has nothing to do with the bill, that when it comes to the construction of branch lines he consider extending the branch line in Saskatchewan from St. Waliburg to Heinsburg, a distance of about forty miles. That is a cut-off which the whole population in that part of Saskatchewan have been begging for, so that they would have a through line from Prince Albert to Edmonton. The proposed branch line in this bill is all right, but we must keep in mind other branch lines. I would also suggest that the Canadian National railway and the Canadian Pacific railway from Peace River west be completed.

I have studied this project fairly thoroughly, and I have come to the conclusion that it is a good one, and one which should be profitable.
The hon. gentleman has asked three questions. With reference to his first question I say to him that the Canadian National railways is not relying exclusively on the factor of population, but it is relying on the natural resources, the timber, agriculture, colonization and fisheries, and upon other indications that were given by the witness before the committee. So far as the soil is concerned I cannot say a great deal more than was said by the witness himself. He is an expert, perhaps one of the best engineers in this country, and he considers that there is a good agricultural area there. It is a clay belt lying to the west of Bell river, and the slope is a gradual one. He goes on further to say that it is a successful agricultural area because people have already established themselves along the transcontinental line north of Barraute.

Mr. Chairman, this matter concerns my constituency. I must say frankly that it is the same old argument which our Tory or Toronto friends have always brought up against the province of Quebec.
I should say, in passing, that this proposed railway line of 47 miles from Barraute northward to Kiask Falls about which we have just heard, will not only supply a paper mill, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said a few moments ago, but it will primarily develop land settlement. And, as has been evidenced for a long time, we have lands suitable for settlement. It should not be forgotten that at the time of my arrival at Amos in 1912, in the very area with which we are now dealing, there was absolutely no development there. Today, we have a population of about 600.000. This goes to show that the area is worthy of being developed. Now, the proposed railway line would serve timber limits containing 6,000,000 cords of pulpwood, and consequently if that line can handle 150,000 cords per year, we may be sure that the receipts will exceed the expenses incurred, and will not cost one cent to the Canadian National Railways.
Profits will be derived from the operation of the railway line from Barraute to the great water power site of Kiask Falls. The profits made will be the same as those which have
always been drawn from our part of the Abitibi district? The Abitibi district and northern Quebec are not responsible for the deficit of the Canadian National Railways; on the contrary, it is rather that area which covers the deficits that have resulted from the fact that too many branch lines have been built in the west and in Ontario, while we never had our share in Quebec.
To me, such charges are truly ridiculous, and show that those who make them are ignorant of facts.
That line will make possible the development of the north country. As is well known, large quantities of ore are to be found in the north. Full particulars have been given during the discussion on gold mining, and everyone knows that the proposed line is essential to the prosperity of this country.
The line will be built not only in the interests of my constituency, but in the interests of the whole province and even of Canada at large, and I hope that this measure will be passed unanimously.

Before this item passes there is a question I should like to ask the minister having to do with the Soldier Settlement Act and the Veterans' Land Act. As we know,
the soldier settlement board has to do mostly with soldiers of the first war, while the Veterans' Land Act has to do with soldiers of the second war who are taking up land or small holdings. There are two organizations, the soldier settlement board and the Veterans' Land Act. I notice that there is one director for the Soldier Settlement Act and the Veterans' Land Act, which is a good thing, but could not this idea be carried through the whole administration of the two acts? The work being done across the country is practically the same, because they are dealing with soldiers and land in the same areas. Why should there be two staffs across Canada to do practically the same work? That does not seem to me to be very economical. I notice on page 256 that there are seven district superintendents under the Veterans' Land Act. I notice also there is a reduction from five to one in the district superintendents, soldier settlement, while there is an added superintendent, agricultural branch. On the same page it states that there are 39 field supervisors, soldier settlement, grade 2, and 54 field supervisors, soldier settlement, grade 1. It would appear that there must be considerable duplication, and it would be in the interests of economy to have the same administration handle both the settlement board and the Veterans' Land Act.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I agree with every word my hon. friend has said. There is a complete merger of the administration of the two acts at the present time. I think my parliamentary assistant will want to supplement what I have said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
What I have to say will also answer the question asked last night in regard to the actual cost of administration of the Soldier Settlement Act. Obviously employees of the soldier settlement board are also doing work which comes under the Veterans' Land Act. The administration of the two acts is fully merged. Some work is being done which might be regarded as strictly attributable to soldier settlement board activities. It is hard to separate them in the estimates when they are working in connection with both acts. When there is one director over these two land settlement acts it is obvious that there cannot be a clear-cut line of demarcation in the office and field services charged to each act. In 1945, when the Veterans' Land Act work made up by far the greater portion of the activities, the department made as close an estimate as possible
Supply-Veterans Affairs

of costs chargeable to each act for the fiscal year- 1945-46. With the greatly improved standing of soldier settlement accounts brought about by the debt adjustment under P.C. 10472, begun in 1943 and still going on, the cost of soldier settlement administration was estimated at $120,000. This estimate for 1945-46 is now confirmed and will stand for the present fiscal year 1946-47. The estimate should be considered on the basis that there is the complete merger suggested by the hon. member for Royal.
In regard to P.C. 10472 our committee recommended that the provisions for applications under that order in council should be extended to September 1, 1946. It was thought by the government that that hardly gave veterans who might wish to apply time enough, so the order in council which was passed on August 8, 1946 extended the time for application under P.C. 10472 to December 31 of this year.
The idea is that eventually both acts will be administered under the one head.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are now, as a matter of fact.
Are the thirty-nine field supervisors, soldier settlement grade 2, doing Veterans' Land Act supervision as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
And the fifty-four, grade 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Is the veteran to be allowed to farm the way he thinks best, or will he be told how to farm by some supervisor who does not know anything about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are regional
advisory committees all across Canada, and he is given the best advice possible consistent with the prospects of his future success in settlement.
Then he is going to be advised every time what to plant, or how to farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
Or when to sell ?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, he is only advised with regard to the reasonable prospects in settlement.
He has been in the past. He has been told what to plant, and how to farm, and all about it, by some supervisor who in many cases did not know anything about farming.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; if he has the personality and the prospects for success he is allowed to develop his own initiative in regard to what he going to do.

During the past few years, as I think the superintendent or director will admit, the habit has grown up of many of the departments of government using the field force of the soldier settlement board for various other purposes,-under the dominion farm loan act and many other government activities. They have been doing a good deal of work for the government other than that which is directly connected with their jobs. That was all right during the period when they were not being overworked, but at the present time that staff should be and I believe is fully occupied in dealing with the new settlers. This work they are doing for the other departments should, I think, be taken off their shoulders. I suggest to the minister that something be done about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend's observations. But the general policy is that the investigations which they make for other departments are not supposed to interfere with their essential obligations in regard to Soldier settlement.

Nevertheless they have only so many hours in the day in which to work, and if they have to make investigations and reports for some other departments it means that part of their time is occupied with those matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, but we have field staffs which do nothing else but these investigations.

The minister will admit that very often these men were employed in other work, and therefore it was almost impossible to get at the actual cost of operating the soldier settlement board. I asked a number of questions with regard to that last night at eleven o'clock, and the minister said he would give the answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The cost of what?
The cost of collections, the administration under the soldier settlement board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have already given the costs. It was very hard to be exact, because, as the hon. member says, the acts are administered together. One of the main reasons for some extra cost of administration is the administration of order in council P.C. 10472, which, as I stated already, has been extended to the end of -this year. The costs are estimated at $120,000. The hon. member

Supply-Veterans Affairs
wanted to know, I believe, the number of cancellations during the last two years. The answer is that there have been five cancellations in that period, and just one of these was an eviction. In many cases the settler moves away and it is necessary to cancel, because a quick claim cannot be obtained from him, or there is some other difficulty, but during the past two years there have been five cancellations or terminations or rescissions, and one of them an eviction.
Has the minister figures showing the relation between the cost of administration or collection by the soldier settlement board and the amount collected?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That was given before the committee. There are extensive tables, for which I would refer the hon. member to pages 336 to 341 inclusive, of the proceedings of the committee on veterans affairs, showing the collections through the whole period. There is there shown collections for the period from April 1, 1945 to March 31, 1946, from April 1, 1944 to March 31, 1945, and so on right up to date. The exact figures are given-the payments, which are made, the prepayments which are made, and by districts; it is a complete and exhaustive statement, and I believe the hon. gentleman will find there everything he wants. I can give the committee, though, the highlights of it. The actual statement of course indicates that the position of the soldier settler contracts has been improved amazingly, particularly during the last four years.	.
War prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, we hope that good prices will continue. It is also the hope of my bon. friend, and I think, a hope which will be realized.
We only hope that it will not be as a result of war.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I think we should pay a tribute to the wonderful work of the soldier settlers when they really get a chance of paying up their accounts, and I am very happy to pay that tribute to them. 'These are the highlights: 2,621 settlers, or one-third of the total active settlers as of March 31, 1942, have repaid their loans in full in cash and received title to their farms. In the four year period soldier settlers paid in cash on their contracts $5,476,489. Of this amount, $3,292,000 was in the form of payments on current instalments, and $2,183,000, prepayments in advance of maturity dates-an amazing record of desire to pay up. A review of the statistics shows that 85 per cent of the
present total of 4,276 soldier settlers should have little difficulty in paying out their loans under the present contracts.
That brings into question P.C. 10472, the right to apply under which has been extended to the end of this year in accordance with the recommendations of our committee. The average age of the soldier settlers is just under fifty-seven years, and the average debt is $1,160.
Would the hon. member give the most recent figure of the number of soldier settlers still on the land who have not yet obtained clear title?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: How nlany of those titles were acquired during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For the calendar year to date, 620.

The answer which I did not get from the minister, although I assume it is in the figures, is the relation between the amount collected from the soldier settlers, particularly in the period say from 1926, and the actual cost of collecting it. I just want it roughly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I will give the figure for the period April 1, 1945 to March 31, 1946. That is the first table here.
That is not what I wanted. I wanted the picture from 1926.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, the whole thing is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member wants a composite percentage relationship?
That is right. I want the amount collected and the cost of collecting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We will get that.

It is important. For
instance, I notice that a group of 750 soldier settlers in Saskatchewan who owed originally $2,800,000 and had paid off a little more than half of that, $1,500,000, find that they still owe the government $3,800,000. Although they paid off more than half of what they originally owed, they now owe more than when they started.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In reply to my hon.
friend's question of a few minutes ago, the estimate of the officials is that the cost of administration is less than one per cent of the expenditure.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member will
get that from the figures I gave. The collections in the last four years were $5,476,000. If you take the average cost of administration at $120,000 per year, you get just about one per cent.

That does not give
the picture for all those years back in the 1930's when wheat was down and inspectors were going all over the country trying to collect and the settlers could not pay anything. This last four years was a very favourable period. I agree with the minister, and I was glad to hear him say it, that these settlers desire more than anything else to pay off their debts. For twenty years and more they have been struggling to do that, and I wish I could get the officials to realize the plight these people are in and to recognize their good intentions. I have a number of cases in my own constituency, with which naturally I am familiar. I received a letter from the wife of one of these soldier settlers not long ago. She wanted to know what could be done to get title to their land. The man and his wife are on a quarter-section of land, and the soldier settlement board refused to grant them title, although they had asked for reductions and had bought and later sold another quarter-section of land and paid the proceeds into the board. The actual figures as given to me were that they had already paid off $3,000 on their land, had bought another quarter-section which they sold at $1,600 and paid that in, but they still could not get title to their own land. The doctor has ordered this soldier, who is getting up in the sixties, to go to a warmer climate. He cannot stand the hard work any longer, and they want to sell their land but cannot get title to it. Is there any machinery in the department whereby this man can dispose of his equity in that land so that he can get out from under and retire, and so that there may be some security for his wife?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The settlers are selling their equity in the land every day.
I will take this particular case to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall be very glad
to look into it.

I hope something
will be done about it, because it is a deserving case.

The picture is clearing up in
connection with the old soldier settlers, and if they live long enough they will perhaps

get title to their land. The soldier settlers have taken the stand right along, as many of us have done who have been trying to help them, that unjust burdens were piled upon them to begin with, and while concessions have been made from time to time by different governments in office, the concessions have never caught up with the difficulties in which these old settlers were placed. The government has dealt leniently with veterans of the last great war, but the veterans of the first great war who still have contracts with the board as of March 31, 1944, have been sadly neglected.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise
to a point of order. My friend and I know this subject very well. He has been very consistent, and devoted in his advocacy, but parliament disposed of this question earlier this session.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, we are considering item 464, which
reads:	.
Administration of soldier settlement, British family settlement, general land settlement and Veterans Land Act, including engineering and other investigational planning and subdivision expenses that do not add tangible value to real property, $5,443,400.	[DOT]
I should like to know why I am to be debarred from discussing what other hon. members right alongside of me have been discussing for the last fifteen minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For the reason that my hon. friend made this question the subject matter of a specific resolution which, was debated and disposed of by the house previously this session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the point of order raised by the minister is well taken. As he says, this matter was discussed under a bill that was brought down in the house, and the decision made then could be changed only, by a resolution of the house. The item under consideration is the administration of soldier settlement, and discussion respecting administration would be in order.
I do not see why I should be singled out from everybody. I understand that we have all the same rights here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The only question my hon. friend is debarred from discussing is the granting of clear title to soldier settlers, which was a specific matter discussed and disposed of by the house previously this session. My hon. friend is not debarred from discussing any other question at all relating to administration.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

I hope to be back next session, when I will deal with the question again in detail, as I have done before. I still protest against the treatment of these old veterans.
I notice that the cost of administration is now estimated at $120,000 a year, in comparison with the cost of $1,100,000 during the first twenty-five years of administration of the act. That huge expenditure looks to me like a lot of money wasted, or inefficiency or whatever you wish to call it. I believe it is partly due to a lack of ministerial supervision of the board during the time Hon. T. A. Crerar was minister. I am glad to see that the present minister is doing a little better so far as administration is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Much better.

I am still looking for something worth, while to be done for these old veterans, and I hope it will be done. I would ask why the cost of administration in. the first twenty-five years was so heavy as compared with now.
A Canadian Press dispatch in the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, August 14, states that the Prime Minister of Canada has intimated that Canada is not going to collect some $10,000,009 of debt which Italy owes us, and yet we are continuing to collect from these old soldier settlers of the first great war. It is just too bad. I know from conversations I have had with the minister that he wants to give these old veterans clear title. I want to know where the unseen power rests which will not allow the veterans to be given clear title. I am very sorry that this parliament is tied down as it is. Next session I am going to be back and if we do not get clear title for the old veterans I will see to it, as far as it is in my power to do so, that the veterans of this war get the treatment to which they are entitled and shall not be abused as the old veterans were.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I certainly admire my hon. friend's consistent attitude on this question.

In the last few days I have had a number of inquiries and expressions of dissatisfaction regarding the Braefoot project in Saanich. I understand the Canadian Legion and the chairman of the rehabilitation council of Victoria have requested an investigation into the administration of that project. I wonder if the minister could say whether an inquiry is being made and an investigation carried out, and if so, whether he has received any report on it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The minister will answer that question in a moment. In the meantime,
with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Battle River, he can take what steps he likes as a member of parliament, but I may tell him that the time for applying for a real cut-down in these old debts of the soldier settlers of world war I has been extended to the end of this year. It may be a further extension will be made; on the other hand it may not be made. No one can be sure of that. It will be a matter of government policy. I would ask my hon. friend however to bear in mind that, if he indicates that clear titles will be given in spite of the decision of parliament again this year against his proposal, and as by that he may cause some of these soldier settlers to defer applying under order in council 10472, he should realize exactly what he may be doing. I do not want to start a controversy, but I am pointing out to him that under the order in council of July 31, 1946, a total of 1,765 settlers have had their .debts reduced by $1,112,000, or an average of $630 per settler. Eighty per cent of the reductions have been made in Saskatchewan and Alberta, where two-thirds of the total settlement is located and where the adversities of the thirties had the greatest impact. The hon. gentleman was not a member of our committee. Had he been he would have heard the evidence of the director that in some cases such sweeping settlements were made under this order in council that sometimes as much as fifty per cent equity was granted to a settler; and in his campaign, which of course he has every right to carry on if he wishes to do so, I would ask him to bear in mind that the ' right to apply under P.C. 10472 has been extended only to the end of the year. It will do no harm for him to remember that, when he advises the various soldier settlers.

I thank the parliamentary assistant for the information given, which I already-had, and I may say that I advised those persons who have written to me in connection with debts that the offer is still open until September 30.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: December 31, 1946.

This is a new intimation I have received to-day. That however does not remove the injustice. There was a good deal of information given in that return, which was supposed to have cost $2,000-Which I do not believe for a moment-showing that great reductions had been made. To my personal knowledge as much as four times the cost of the land at the time the sales were made in my- own district has been charged these men,
Supply-Veterans Affairs

and it will take a good deal of the fifty ,per cent reduction to equalize the injustice imposed on the old veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In reply to the member for Nanaimo, I may say that prices are all being revised in connection with these properties. All the lands have been disposed of. There are a few who are dissatisfied with the settlement and the matter is still under consideration.
To what time has the date for applications been extended?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Under P.C. 10472? To
December 31 of this year. It is further than the committee asked for.

It will be remembered that in 1942, when the act was first introduced, the former board under the old soldier settlement act were bitterly criticized on the ground that they had settled men who should not have been settled, and also settled men on land that was not really suitable. There was harsh criticism on that ground, and now as a consequence we find that the officials of the Veterans Land Act are overcautious in deciding what men should be allowed to go on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As recommended by the committee of 1942.

I realize it is the result of the criticism we made. They are being a little too cautious. I suggest that there should be a margin beyond which they should not go. So long as a man can qualify from the point of view' of experience; so long as he can qualify by reason of character, so long as he has the necessary money to put up the ten per cent, I do not think any veteran should be debarred from coming under the Veterans Land Act on the ground that his financial resources are not sufficient to enable him to succeed. If he has the experience, the ability, the character, the money to put down ten per cent, and can get-suitable land, he should not be debarred merely on the ground that his chances of success are small. But men have been debarred for that reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend.	.

I had to be in another committee last night and it may be that some information was given with regard to the disposition of the million dollars voted to equalize the costs of small holdings across the country. Was that information given? The point is this. In the committee we tried to find out how that money would be spent and how the costs would be equalized, and

we were told that final costs had not been submitted by the directors of the small holdings schemes, which were being built on the cost plus basis, and therefore the final figures as to the cost of houses could not be given. Have the final figures been submitted, and may we have an idea of the average cost of the most expensive house in the -country under the small holdings scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Up to the present time just about half of that million dollars has been allotted. I am not in a position at the moment to give the final disposition of the areas and the allotments in respect of the remainder.
Can the minister or his assistant give information as to what will be the average highest cost-87,500 or $8,000- when the adjustment has been made?
The hon. member will find that in the table I put on Hansard last night.
Can the hon. member give it to me now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The average cost, in the statement put on Hansard yesterday, in regard to the 2,706 units, is, on the basis of the best figures we have so far, $5,969 for the house only. With various services, which include land, water., sewer service, temporary heating, transportation, travel time, drainage, driveways, roads, landscaping, and all other costs to the director, the total average unit cost was $7,058.51. The average cost of those under $6,000, house only, was $5,574.34. The average cost of those over $6,000, house only, was $6,394.17. The average excess per house over $6,000 was $213.36.
I think I am correct in saying 'that in no case is the down payment being increased, but the extra cost will be amortized over the twenty-five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct, at three and a half per cent.
These figures were given last night?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; and the rental cost to the householders over twenty-five years was given by my assistant in the house last night.

Yes. The final point I wish to make is this. It has been stated that before they are allowed in the house some veterans are required to give an undertaking that they will pay whatever the excess over $6,000 may be. Apparently it has not been

Supply-Veterans Affairs
made clear to them that this excess will be amortized over the years, and that therefore they are not going to have to pay $1,300, or whatever the extra amount is. I know that situation exists because I have had personal information from the pla.ce where one of these holdings is situated. I wish the government could make it clear to all veterans that there will be a small extra payment monthly, and I wish the minister would put into effect our recommendation as to the subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct.
Will the minister make that clear?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact the hon. member is quite right as to the extra payments in these cases being spread over twenty-five years. Formerly anything over the $6,000 had to be paid in addition to the cash payment. That was changed by the amendment which we passed and the order in council which was also passed some time ago whereby $600 had to be paid down and the remainder amortized. Of course it may be that somebody has not received that information, or has not been fully apprised of it; but there is no doubt that it will be made clear that the payments will be $600 down in regard to the small holdings which have already been built and the whole amount over the $600 will be spread out over the twenty-five years, less the conditional grant.

I wish to concur in what the hon. member for Acadia has said with regard to numbers of veterans failing to qualify for financial reasons. I believe, as he does, that where a veteran has a good character, has farming experience and the ten per cent, there should be no question of his being qualified under the act.
I also wish to raise a point in respect to the values of land being purchased under the Veterans Land Act. In the district I represent the practice being followed is to take the 1941 price of land in that area as the basis on wrhich the board would purchase land. If the vendors ask a price greater than that, the board insists that the applicant or the soldier shall himself put up the difference between the price that is asked and the price that the board will pay. That is working a hardship on a great many veterans, and it does not give a fair picture of the cost of land to the veterans in that area, because in many cases the veterans are paying the difference between the price asked and the price which the board are prepared to pay under the plan. I am not contending that the 63260-309
board should go out and pay any price at all for land, but I think anybody who has followed the agricultural trend during the last three or four years will agree that based on our present agricultural prices there is an added value to land over the 1941 prices. The board would be justified in raising the sights a little on the price which they are prepared to pay for good land in good crop areas. If they did that I believe they could settle a greater number of veterans than are being settled at the present time.
A point was raised by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton with regard to the advice given to settlers going on the land. There should be a closer liaison between the department's supervisors and the agricultural representatives in the various provinces. They are the people who should be giving advice to the settlers settling under the Veterans Land Act, rather than the supervisors. I suggest that the closest liaison be maintained between the agricultural representatives of the various provinces and the supervisors. Let these people give the advice to the settler with regard to agricultural practices. They know the practices better than the supervisor; they are in a better position to advise, and I believe that their advice will be taken with better grace than it will be from the supervisors.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I tell my hon. friend that there is the closest cooperation and constant consultation with the provincial government agricultural representatives at the present time, and between our supervisors and our regional advisory committee.

I have spoken on this question at different times, having had some experience with the building of houses on small holdings. Does the minister believe that this type of housing is meeting the requirements of the veterans? I ask this question because I wras on a committee which looked in to the housing act. We made a survey in my district. We asked those who would like to build under the National Housing Act, the small holdings and the wartime housing. We found that practically all of the men favoured wartime housing because they could rent the houses at approximately $30 a month, which would give them a reasonable time to find their feet and know what they intended to do over a period of a few years. Under the small holdings arrangements, or the National Housing Act, it took practically all of their gratuity to make the down payment, which left them with very little money to set up housekeeping, buy furniture and all the things that are necessary to that end. The small holdings built in my district are not yet

Supply-Veterans Affairs

completed, and it seems as if no applications have been made to occupy these houses. It would appear that it is not the type of house which meets the requirements or the need of the veteran. Under this housing scheme would it be possible to bring in a system similar to wartime housing by which a veteran could rent the house for a few years until he knows where he is and) what he wants to do and whether he will have sufficient money at that, time to build a house when materials will be available and he will be better established? Doe3 the minister think that plan would work?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All the housing work of Canada is now being co-ordinated under the general direction of the Minister of Reconstruction, with consultations with our department and the Department of Finance. My own personal opinion-and I am not an expert on housing; I have been through many of our houses-with all respect to my colleague who is not here, is that *wartime housing houses do not compare with ours. I wish my hon. friend could visit British Columbia and see the first ten that were built in Canada on Lulu island. In artistic design, symmetry of construction, and convenience for living they are absolutely the best I have seen. To my mind the other ones are rather rigid. They are all of a pattern such as you would see in England and Scotland under the county council scheme. They look like a series of trench houses; they are all the same. That is the thing to avoid. In housing every design should be different, in order to give the houses that symmetry in construction which is more acceptable to the occupant. If you go out to Lulu island you will see that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
May I say a word in reply to the hon. member for Melfort? The difficulty arising from the increase in land values is constantly being considered by the administration and advisory committees. I am in entire agreement with everything he said in that regard and I believe the administration is trying to deal with the situation as well as it can, without contributing too much to an undue inflation in land values.
At one oclock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer again to the small holdings scheme under the Veterans Land Act, and particularly to the thirty or forty housing projects which the government has undertaken. In the figures which he gave last night, and again 
to-day, the parliamentary assistant has shown that for the most expensive group of houses, those costing over $6,000, the average cost would be $7,058. That would be after the $1,000,000 has been applied to adjusting costs across the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is before the
$1,000,000 has been applied.

I understood from the
parliamentary assistant that it was after.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the cost.

Considerable confusion
exists in this matter. I have received information by telephone, which was checked previously with officials of the department, to the effect that some of these houses are going to cost the veteran as much as $7,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

I think the minister and his senior officials should check with the officials in the various regions. In this instance I am referring to the Sherbrooke district. The information I have received is that a five-room house which was originally supposed to cost $4,800 will now cost $7,300, and that the price of a six-room house has increased $1,800 over the original $6,000. In fairness I should add that my informant told me that the officials of the Veterans' Land Act could not or would not give him firm final figures. This was the best information that was available to the veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. gentleman?-and I do this in an effort to be helpful. The actual cost to a veteran would be the gross cost less the contingent additional grant of $1,400, less again the .amount of the write-off which may be arranged under the $1,000,000.

I am glad the minister pointed that out. I inadvertently said that the total cost to the veteran would be $7,300, but I should have said the total cost of the house will be $7,300. That is an increase of $1,300 over what was previously thought to be the maximum of $6,000.
Figures given last night as to the adjusted cost in monthly payments showed that the maximum monthly payment would be something like $27 a month for twenty-five years, at which time the total cost would be amortized. The significant fact is that the house which the veteran expected to obtain for a maximum cost of $6,000, less the additional write-off of $1,400, now will cost $1,300 or $1,400 more. Instead of the veteran being left with a liability of $4,800, he will be left, with a liability rf $6,000. In effect he

Supply-Veterans Affairs
will have a mortgage of $6,000. It is stated that this is to be amortized over twenty-five years and the cost will not be more than $27 a month, but the point is that these veterans assumed that they were going to be able to obtain houses with an outstanding liability of not more than $4,800. In the case of the smaller house, they assumed that the liability would not be more than $3,500 or $4,000; they are now faced with liabilities of from $4,500 to $6,000. These liabilities, it is true, may be amortized, but the fact remains that these veterans will have large mortgages hanging over their heads.
The arrangements outlined by the parliamentary assistant for amortization are perhaps the best that can be made if the government will not adopt the suggestion to advance the subsidy and underwrite the proportion of the cost over $6,000. What should be done is to apply the same subsidy to the proportion of the cost in excess of $6,000 as is now applied to the proportion of the cost under $6,000.
I bring up this matter again because veterans throughout the country are worried at the extent of the liabilities they are called upon to assume. It is not good enough to say that they are getting a better deal under this scheme than they are under any other. The fact is that they have made their arrangements; they are not able to make any other arrangements. They have gone ahead on the assumption that they would take the house and they expected to move into it; in some cases they have actually given up other tenancies. Instead of being faced with a reasonable obligation which they could hope to pay off, they are going to have to assume an obligation of some $4,500 for the lowest priced houses and $6,000 for the higher priced houses.
I appreciate the fact that the minister and his department have made an effort to adjust this by limiting the down payment to S600 and leaving the excess to be amortized over twenty-five years. I give them credit for going that far, but it is not far enough. The department has led the veteran to assume that he would 'be able to get a house which would cost a maximum of $6,000, and now it is found that it will cost almost a minimum of $6,000. I submit that the government has an obligation to these veterans, because they have been given that impression as a result of the government's representation.
I can say no more other than to press on the minister the desirability of adopting the recommendation of the committee that the cost over $6,000 be subsidized to the same degree as the cost under $6,000.

I do not think there is much point in pursuing these figures, because they were given on the spur of the moment; but if that is the average cost to the veteran it is a good deal less than under the Veterans Land Act. My criticism applies only to projects built on a cost-plus basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The figure I gave was the initial deposit. The rest is provided from their own private resources.

That is not what I was complaining of. A veteran makes a contract on his own for a house. He is willing to assume payment for a $6,000 house. He knows what he is getting. But here he pays dowrn 1600 and expects to get a $6,000 house, but. he is now advised that he must assume a $7,000 house or he will lose his S600. That is what I am complaining about, where houses have been built on a cost-plus basis and the costs have increased beyond what the veteran was led to expect. I do not see that the figure given by the minister showing that the veteran has had to pay $100 more than his credit has any bearing on the matter, because under the scheme I refer to the veteran pays down $600, which is $200 more than his reestablishment credit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Many veterans go out into the market and buy their own houses with this reestablishment credit of $425 on the average. Building costs have risen, as everybody knows. We are already giving a conditional grant of $1,400 to the veteran on the small holding, but these veterans are in the proportion of one to five of the veterans who are investing money in housing. If we go further and give the veteran who is receiving a conditional grant of $1,400 further assistance, the five out of six who are investing in housing outside of the Veterans Land Act would have just cause for complaint, because they get no help at all except their reestablishment credit. There has to be some equity in all these schemes. I can understand the hon. member's attitude in bringing this matter up, but the case is similar to the farm lands case which was brought up by the hon. member for Mel-fort, who said that land which you could have bought for $8,000 three years ago costs $12,000 to-day. Is the state to step in and pay the difference? That is a question that has to be considered in reference to what is being done for other veterans. The veterans who are providing houses for themselves are facing the same increased building costs, and if we say to the veterans under the Veterans Land Act: "We are already giving you $1,400 and now we are going to give you even more," the man who is getting only his reestablishment credit would have cause for complaint.

I think it has been conclusively established that in the housing projects built on a cost-plus basis the increase over what you might call the normal costs has been greater than where the veteran has made a private deal for the building of a house. The director under the Veterans Land Act has said that he would not let any more cost-plus contracts, fMr. Mackenzie.]
and I am glad of that. That indicates that experience has proved that building costs have increased more in these cost-plus projects than they have elsewhere. All I am asking is that that fact be recognized and that the veteran be put in the position he had assumed he would be in as a result of the government's representations made to him in good faith, and who now is faced with these increased costs in these projects built on the cost-plus basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We called for tenders in all these housing projects and we found a definite lack of cooperation from the contractors in tendering, and so we were compelled to go ahead on what we call a fixed-fee basis of $200 per house right across Canada. We tried to get tenders all across Canada in the first instance, but the contractors were chary of venturing into these housing projects for veterans.

The hon. member for

speechtext: If the hon. member did not say that, I understood he thought it. He is getting the $1,400 write-off; he is getting the advantage of a house built under lower prices than those which prevail to-day, and he is possibly getting some advantage under the million dollar write-off.

I have in mind a small Indian reserve and band. The example they gave during the

recent war, and perhaps during the previous great war, is a remarkable example of patriotism and allegiance to British ideals. On section 15-new part VIIIA.

Under section 15 (1) we have certain lengthy provisions extending over more than three pages. What I have

to say will apply equally to all the new sections which are proposed to be inserted in the act. The key to the new proposed appeal procedure is in some respects found in the new section 69F, at page 28, where we find a provision which embodies the budget resolutions. It provides:
This part and the schedules referred to in this part are applicable only in respect of assessments of income of the nineteen hundred and forty-six and subsequent taxation years and part \ III of tills act is not applicable in respect of the said assessments.
I do not wish to occupy the time of the committee in a repetition of the observations I made in the debate on the budget resolutions. I must repeat, however, that in large measure, the provision in 69F reduces to futility the new provisions for appeal procedure. It comes down to this, that on the 1946 income the taxpayer will make his return in the spring of 1947. The assessment, in the ordinary course, will reach him about the year 1950. This new appeal procedure does not begin to function until after the taxpayer has received his notice of assessment which, in the ordinary course of events, he will receive about 1950 for the first year to which this new appeal procedure can apply.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We will try to speed up the assessment.
It will take a lot of speeding up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I agree.

But let us be very hopeful, perhaps unduly hopeful, and say that the notice of assessment might be expected in two years or, if we strain our imaginations, a year and a half. Even so, it still means that it will be 1949 before the new appeal procedure can have any opportunity to function.
If there is merit in this new appeal procedure-and I think it is the opinion of the committee that such procedure is long overdue ; it certainly was the opinion of the senate committee which made very useful recommendations-then surely that appeal procedure should be put to work now. Here we are about to pass legislation to bring into being two new bodies with appellate powers. We are to have an income tax appeal board and an income tax advisory board; and yet these bodies are not to begin to function until about 1950, in the ordinary course of events. If it is greatly speeded up, it might begin to work in 1949. If this procedure is not to become effective for another three years, why should we be asked to pass it now? On the other hand, if there is merit in this appeal procedure, and there is a need for it, it ought

to be available to the taxpayer now. That is my first observation respecting section 15.
My second relates to cases which involve appeals, both from decisions on facts or law and from decisions involving the exercise of the minister's discretion. I am not going to go into the subject of the exercise of discretion because I discussed that on a previous occasion. However, I should like to put before the minister a case for which it seems to me no provision has been made in section 15. Take a case which might arise under both sections 69A and 69B. Suppose an appeal is launched under section 69A to the income tax appeal board from an assessment. Let us assume that one of the points involved in the minister's decision has to do with one of the subjects in connection with which he is entitled to exercise discretion under the act. In that event presumably the appeal would lie under section 69E to the other board, the income tax advisory board. It seems to me that no provision has been made here for the case which involves a decision on a point of fact or law and a decision involving the exercise of discretion. In other words, no provision has been made for the double-barrelled case. The scheme of procedure laid down in this section is that where an appeal does not involve the exercise of the minister's discretion, the appeal will lie from the minister to the income tax appeal board. But where issue is taken by the taxpayer with the minister's exercise of one of his discretionary powers, the appeal will be taken to the income tax advisory board, which does not render a judgment but simply advises the minister. The procedures in the two cases are different. The results which might flow from the decisions of the two boards are different. I therefore submit that further consideration should be given to cases involving both types of decision.
The third observation I should like to make is with reference to the draftsmanship of the substantive sections dealing with the powers of the appeal boards in these various cases. It may be that because a number of new provisions are being inserted following the present section 69 resort had to be had to schedules, but it seems to me to be an unfortunate departure from sound draftsmanship to relegate to schedules sections of the highest importance defining the powers of these appeal boards and the extent of their jurisdiction. Let us agree that schedules are the proper place to set out rates of taxation and such matters, but they are not the place to find substantive provisions of a statute defining the powers of boards of appeal. As I say, it may be that the draftsman felt that as he was inserting in the act a code of procedure

between two sections, he did not wish them to extend to too great a length. If this bill is to be enacted in its present form I would urge upon the minister that when the time comes to revise the act these provisions be put in their proper place so that the sections defining the jurisdiction of these boards of appeal will follow the sections dealing with appeals in general.
The next observation I should like to make relates to warning the taxpayer of his rights in the matter of appeal. It is not to be expected that great numbers of taxpayers will know the new law with reference to appeals, particularly as we are now to have various forms of appeal. My request is that the new appeal procedure be made effective by giving the taxpayer warning in each case of his appeal rights. In the first instance, take the notice of assessment. I suggest that the notice of assessment bear on its face a warning as to what are the rights of appeal from the assessment. The taxpayer should be told that under the provisions of section 69A he may within two months appeal to the minister. Then when he receives the minister's decision he should be warned in that decision that he may within three months appeal to the income tax appeal board. The judgment issued by that board should in turn warn him that he has four months to appeal to the exchequer court. Similarly in cases involving the exercise of the minister's discretion, the taxpayer should be notified that under section 69E he may within two months file his notice of objection with . the minister. Then if the minister rejects his appeal, under subsection 3 of section 69E he may within two months require the minister to refer the case to the income tax advisory board.	.
I should like to conclude these remarks with one further observation. In section 69B, subsection 1, paragraph (b), there is a provision which I think should be carefully examined. This is the section outlining the right of appeal to the income tax appeal board, and two cases are provided for. First, an appeal may be launched after the minister has confirmed the assessment or reassessed. Second, an appeal may be launched after six months have elapsed after service of the notice of objection and the minister has not notified the taxpayer that he has vacated or confirmed the assessment or reassessed. That section comes down to this: If for any reason the board comes to the conclusion that there is no merit in the appeal, or if the appeal is ignored by the department, or if it has not received the taxpayer's notice of appeal and the department gives no notice to the taxpayer that no action is being taken 63260-3104
on his appeal, then the taxpayer's rights of appeal are gone without any notice to him whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This section is to protect the taxpayer.

It deals with the case of the minister not having notified the taxpayer after he has vacated the assessment or reassessed, and it will apply in the case where a taxpayer has served his notice of objection and nothing happens for six months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: May I just try to clear that up? Under this section the taxpayer would first appeal to the minister and the minister may confirm the assessment or reassess. If he appeals to the minister and the minister does nothing for six months, if the minister just sits on it and the taxpayer hears nothing, then after the expiry of the six months he can go to the appeal board. It is really to give . the minister six months in which either to handle the objection or fail to do it. There is really a six months' term for the taxpayer. In other words, the minister is given six months to straighten the thing out before the taxpayer goes to the income tax appeal board. While the drafting may not be perfect, that is the purpose of the section and' I think it fairly accurately sets out that intention.

The appeal by the taxpayer may not involve a large amount, and he may not have legal advice in connection with his right to appeal. He submits his notice of objection to the minister, and then he waits to hear from the minister. Six months pass.

speechtext: My hon. friend is correct in that last statement. And earlier years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

I have carefully considered that point and1 have discussed it with the officers of the department and considered the possibilities of doing what my hon. friends have suggested, but I am afraid it is not feasible to do so, for this reason. The present procedure of appeal to the exchequer court will remain available for those prior years.
Some progress is being made in expediting the assessment of returns. The average at present is about nine months to a year on individual returns. I must confess that that includes the easy returns, the small salary returns. For the larger returns made by people with other sources of income, where the assessment is more complicated, I do not pretend that the average is as short as I have mentioned; it is longer. [Mr. Fleming.!
functions under the act? Ot is it the government's intention not to appoint the income tax appeal board and the advisory board for that period of time, until there has been some reorganization within the department?

Would the minister take a wager on that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Oh, I am not a gambling man. Another interesting point my hon. friend raised was the parallel functions of the advisory board and the income tax appeal board, that appeals may well involve one point in which discretionary power is exercised by the advisory board and other points of fact and of law to go before the appeal board. That situation was thought of, and it was considered that one of two things should be done; that an appeal should be made to the advisory board and get that disposed of first, and the other appeal, if it were thought necessary in order to preserve a time limit, would not be determined until the advisory board had rendered its decision. Or, alternatively, they might proceed on parallel lines, the final decision by the appeal board on questions of fact and of law to await the final determination on the discretionary end. As a lawyer my hon. friend will appreciate that, and it seemed to be the most practical way of approaching it. I think it will be found that the appeals on matters of discretion can be disposed of more expeditiously than the other appeals, because the questions involved, while important, will be of much narrower compass. So I think in practice that is the way it will work out. It was felt in any event that it would be well to experiment to see how it works out on that basis, and if it were found that there was a serious tie-up for reasons such as my hon. friend has suggested, some appropriate change could be made.

Will that not make the appeal procedure expensive and cumbersome? speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

As to drafting and the use of the device of a schedule, I have considerable sympathy with my hon. friend's views on that, and when a general revision of the act is taking place I think we could attempt to see that the necessary provision is made. I am also in complete agreement with him on the advisability of advising the taxpayer of his new rights of appeal, and I feel sure that the Department of National Revenue can adopt procedure along the line he suggested, namely, that a clear statement of the taxpayer's rights of appeal can go out on or accompanying the notice of assessment form.

I have one question to ask the minister which, I think, could properly come at this moment by reason of what the minister has said referring to the revision of the act. May 1 draw his attention to what was said on October 12 last by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Speaking of reorganization, he said-Hansard, page 1006:
Any reorganization of the personal income tax must be so carefully and thoroughly done that it will not have to be re-done in the early future. I have somewhat reluctantly reached the conclusion that, at this early date and in

I would like to know where the matter stands, as it is of public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not the minister's statement before me, although I remember listening to it. Of course in addition to that there is the rearrangement of the act itself. Work is being done on' it continuously. As no one will appreciate better than my hon. friend or other hon. members who have legal training, that is a very big job, it is a difficult job, but work is being done on it steadily. I am not in a position to make any promises, but I vvould certainly hope that the revision, consolidation-simplification, if you want to call it so-to which we have all been looking forward will not be long delayed. I do not think there is anything more I can add to that statement at the moment.
As I understand it, then, one can be assured that this is not something which, is being done in somebody's spare time, but is regarded as an important project which is continuously proceeding.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend can rest assured that that is so.

I am not going to repeat the arguments which I made on August 13 when this matter was referred to on a previous occasion. As I see the situation, while a right of appeal is granted under section 69A, having regard to the subsequent paragraph, section 69E, which deals with the question of the review of discretion, the right of appeal is very greatly circumscribed. While it will in some degree remove some of the objections which have been taken here before, I submit that it does not go far enough. For if discretionary power remains subject to appeal merely subject to submission to an advisory board, with no power to alter the decision madte by the official in the exercise of his discretion, the right of appeal is

to all intents and purposes, in so far as discretion is concerned1, a matter of form and not of effect.
I advanced several arguments the other day-in this matter. It affects individuals everywhere in this country. I come from an agricultural province, and it affects in great measure the farmers not only of my own province but of all over the dominion. Within the last two years intensified efforts have been made by the Department of National Revenue to collect income tax from farmers. Many of them have no records, and because they have none, officials of the income tax branch have simply set arbitrary figures as to what the income was, and upon the basis of whatever the arbitrary figure might be the assessment has been made. And that decision is final, regardless of equities and regardless of any injustice which may have been done.
This whole question, as I said the other day, was dealt with by a committee of the seriate to which reference was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Eglinton. This committee covered the situation thoroughly, and I am going to refer to one or two recommendations which were made and ask the minister whether or not he is prepared to accept an amendment which will provide once and for all a right of appeal and will be in fact a right of appeal for most of the matters upon which to-day ministerial discretion or official discretion is accepted as final. In the report of the special committee of the senate, page 382, the following appears:
The first important consideration which appeared repeatedly throughout the hearings and which is felt to be a fundamental principle in this connection is that the board of tax appeals, when established in whatever form considerd desirable, should be entirely divorced from and independent of the control of that department of government which is charged with the levying and collecting of taxes.
I suhmit that in so far as the advisory board is concerned the bill goes contrary to that principle, which is a necessary principle to be accepted, that justice is to be assured. Second, the senate committee has pointed out that it is equally important-
-that the administering officials of the department which levies and collects the taxes be not accorded any authority relating to the exercise of administrative or ministerial discretion, the levying of assessments, or the imposition of penalties which is not subject to the immediate, effective and conclusive jurisdiction of an independent tribunal.
When one looks at section 69E, setting forth as it does the number of cases of discretion provided for in this act, some indication is given of the small ambit in which there is the right of appeal. As a matter of fact the Acting Minister of Finance has just

stated that, in actions he has had before the courts, they dealt mainly if not exclusively with questions of law. I can well understand that, because if they were matters of discretion there would be no right on the part of the exchequer court to hear those matters unless under the authorities it was established by the objecting party that the discretion had not- really been exercised in a legal manner, or had not been exercised honestly or fairly, or that the person who exercised the discretion did so on the basis of extraneous considerations which ought not to have been before the officer in question. So the result is that the only appeals that would come before the exchequer court, the law being what it is, would be appeals dealing with a matter of law.
