speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I may reply briefly to the points raised by my hon. friend, particularly with reference to the exercise of discretionary powers by the minister under the provisions of the act, It was dealt with by each of us the other diay on second reading of the bill, and I then put forward the view of the government, giving the reasons why it was felt that these discretionary powers must continue to be exercised by a responsible minister of the crown and not by any independent board.
It seems to me that the exercise of discretionary powers, to the extent that this may be necessary, properly belongs to ministers of the crown, and, of course, the government as a whole must take responsibility for the act of any minister, as this government is quite prepared to do. I do not believe that independent bodies that are not responsible to parliament, not responsible to the electors, should exercise the functions of government.
I agree with what has been said in this debate on previous occasions, that these discretions should be restricted to the greatest extent possible, but either under the head of effective administration of an act of this kind- or in the exercise of discretion to determine what is after all a matter of government policy, I think that it is necessary that someone should- have the power to exercise discretion.
Let me give one or two examples, first on the question of depletion. Under the act as it now stands the minister is given the right to fix rates of depletion in the case of certain wasting assets. In my judgment that is in essence a -matter of government policy to be determined by a minister of the crown responsible to parliament and not to be determined by any independent board. The same applies to the question of rates of depreciation. That may not be quite as evident, but again-, in my opinion,-it is only an opinion but -it is my judgment-that is a matter which should be exercised by a responsible minister, a minister responsible to the -people, and not by an independent board. The same -would apply to one of the discretionary powers given under the act, to approve a particular pension fund or plan as being a plan which is entitled to avail of the provisions of the act, As to the appropriate allowance for a reserve for bad debts, there, again, that to me -is a matter of government policy and should be determined by the minister and not by any independent board. There are a number of minor discretions: the power to designate where books and records are to be kept, the right to nominate persons who shall make the return on behalf of a corporation, the general power to enlarge
Income War Tax

returns, and so on. I will not assert that there are not some discretionary powers in the act which should not be eliminated, and we are endeavouring to do that. I do not think there are many. I say that the great majority of the discretions conferred on the minister by the act are discretions which should be conferred on a minister of the crown and not upon any outside independent board which is responsible to no one.
The senate committee did extremely valuable work. They made a thorough investigation of this question. Their report has been most valuable, and in many respects it is being implemented in this legislation; but in my opinion they were mistaken in their recommendation with respect to the exercise of these discretionary powers. I should like to read to the committee one statement which they made in that connection and which will be found at page 383 of the report which the hon. member for Lake Centre read. I wish the committee would listen attentively. This is what it says:
In this connection it is also recommended that the board should, for the purpose of entertaining and disposing of appeals from assesments, have the statutory authority to exercise all the powers and discretions of whatever nature as may now be vested in the Minister of National Revenue under any of the provisions of the Income War Tax Act or the Excess Profits Tax Act, 4940, or any such powers as may be imported into them at any subsequent time by legislative or administrative authority.
I have heard a great deal in this house and elsewhere in the not too distant past about delegating authority to boards; and I would ask hon. members to read that recommendation rather carefully and see whether they do not think the suggestion is that we should delegate to this board, which would be independent of any parliament, independent of the people, the power to exercise discretions in matters which, in my judgment, are matters of government policy. If the discretion is to be exercised it should be exercised by a responsible minister of the crown who sits in the house and must answer for the exercise of that discretion. I do not want to overemphasize that point, but that is the reason why the government has come to the conclusion that' these discretionary powers must be exercised by the responsible minister. In order to give some assurance that these powers will not be exercised arbitrarily, we are proposing to set up this independent advisory board which will have the task of reviewing the exercise of the discretionary powers by a minister, and. if it disagrees with the minister, so stating. But in the final analysis the decision will rest with the responsible minister. If 
he sees fit to do so he can disregard the advice of the advisory board. I think it is fair to say that he would be a bold man to do so. He would have to feel pretty sure that the board had gone astray. Nevertheless he will retain that right, which is fundamental to our system of parliamentary government of taking the action on his responsibility.
Would the minister permit a question?

Would the decision or recommendation of the board on a matter of discretion be made known to the person appealing?

speechtext: Oh, yes; it is our intention that it be made known to the person appealing. It Should be made known not only to him but to the public. It is' the intention that the findings of this advisory board should be made available not only to the person appealing but to the general public. I think it should be helpful to the general public to know how the discretionary powers on matters of policy and otherwise are being interpreted, how they are being exercised, and that parliament should know it. That is the reason, as concisely as I can give it, why the government has decided that these powers must remain with the responsible minister. It is for that reason that I cannot accept the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Lake Centre.

In cases described by the minister as matters of government policy I would find it difficult to disagree with what he has said. In regard to the discretions mentioned in section 69E, has there been singled out of the many discretions which the minister may exercise those which are in fact considered to be matters of government policy? Let me give an example.
I refer the minister to page 17 of the bill and to the discretion reserved to the minister under subsection 2 of section 5, which says that depreciation may be allowed if the taxpayer is, in the opinion of the minister, making a new investment and so on. Is that what the minister would describe as a matter of government policy? It would seem to me to be something different from that. It would seem to me to be a matter not of government policy but merely of interpreting, as a matter of fact, a business point which the act sets out.

speechtext:

one of them. I have had some experience in this line, as my hon. friend knows, and I make the assertion that the discretions which are important, the ones which really affect, the taxpayer in his pocketbook, are ones which relate to government policy.

Let me ask one further question. When the minister says that questions of depreciation or bad debts are matters of government policy, does he mean consideration of depreciation, or bad debt reserves in a particular company or does he mean fixing a general policy which has to be followed and applied in all cases?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
What I mean is fixing a
general policy that is applied in all cases, fixing rates of depreciation and depletion. Particularly in the case of depreciation it is difficult in a statute, for instance, to lay down a general rule for every type of asset. Generally speaking, machinery and equipment is depreciated at, let us say ten per cent a year as an example. But there may be special types of machinery and equipment that depredate much more rapidly. There should be a discretion in the minister to allow that more rapid rate of depreciation. That is what I mean by the exercise of discretion in what is in essence a matter of government policy.

I just want to draw to the attention of the minister a condition which has existed on the interior lakes of British Columbia for a great many years on the Arrow, the Slocan and the Kootenay

lakes, and more particularly, present conditions on the Arrow lakes. The Canadian Pacific. The people in the district are very much inconvenienced and very much perturbed, because, the railway having been promised to them, they flocked into that area in great numbers, and are now in difficulties because the railway has not been completed, and they are asking that this shall be done. If the minister has anything to say on this matter I think that, rather than make a speech at the present time, I will pause here and ask him if he has any further comments to make. Last year consideration was promised, but apparently nothing further has been done; that is, nothing further as far as construction is concerned has been done, although I believe that further surveys and inspections have been made of that district to set just where the line should go.	.

The hon. gentleman is referring, I take it, to the gap between Heins-burg, Alberta, and Frenchman Butte, Saskatchewan, having a mileage of about forty miles. The gap must be considered in the light of the policy of the Canadian National Railways, which is to look, first of all, at the cost of construction; next, at the natural resources in the area, and, finally, at the amount of traffic that is to be derived therefrom. That is the general practice or custom in the railway. There may be, in fact there have been exceptions to it, but on the whole that is the practice which the railway follows with reference to branch lines. To deal more particularly with this line, it has made a survey which indicates that, because of the limited traffic to be derived therefrom, the operation would not be a profitable one. I think that was the
line about which a delegation waited upon me some time ago. I told the delegation pretty much what I had already said to my hon. friend and what I am saying now, and they countered with the suggestion that perhaps a certain angle of that area had not been taken into consideration, that in their estimation there was more traffic to be derived from the area to be closed than the survey of the Canadian National would seem to indicate. So, having regard to that, I asked the railway if they would not take another look at the situation and they have done so, but I am not in a position to give a final report on the conclusion of the survey, except to say that the territory is one which would not produce sufficient traffic to give the Canadian National Railways a return on its investment if the gap were filled by the completion of the line.
At the same time the matter is still under review, of the possibility of the railway being able to serve that territory. The hon. gentleman will remember too the discussion on the Peace River line, when something was said about coordinating rail and highway facilities; and it may very well be, though I am not saying so, that this particular gap is one which might be considered with reference to the coordination of those two facilities. If that were the case it could not be done without the consent of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan or without further consideration of the points raised by the delegation which called to see me in connection with additional traffic. It has not been possible to complete the survey in that respect. That is about as full a report as I can give to my hon. friend on the question.

tou is one of the best paying pieces of branch line of the Canadian National system. It is difficult to say that the forty-mile gap is not going to be a paying proposition. That is parallel to saying that a bridge over a river, because it does not produce any particular traffic, is not a paying proposition. Nothing can be gathered immediately on either side of the bridge, but if these forty miles were filled in the traffic would increase by reason of that very fact. At the present time the people in that area are having to cross the river by means of a ferry to a little branch line on the Canadian Pacific which is some miles south of the river, and a good deal of the trade is laboriously taken that way. At present the handicap is serious, and it seems to me a foolish idea to build so many hundreds of miles of railway and' leave that forty-mile gap in the middle.

When this question came up for discussion last year I added my words to those of hon. members who spoke in favour of it. The line is not in my constituency, but many of the people in my riding have written letters to me in connection with the matter, because they are put to a good deal of extra trouble and expense on account of the gap not being finished. The minister has given reasons why the line should not be finished, but the service that ought to be given the people there is something that should be taken into consideration, because dollars and cents do not make up the whole story. I would urge again: that this forty-mile gap be completed as soon as possible, because it is highly desirable that the country there should be developed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I endeavour to call members as I see them rise, but sometimes a number of members rise from one group, and I try to call others who rise from other groups so that one group will not monopolize the discussion.

Coming from Nova Scotia, I wish to bring up one matter that is of importance to us in that part of the country, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I am not going to discuss maritime freight rates. I am not -being critical of the railway or of the employees, for I realize the great service that the employees have given the country,
TMr. Townley-Smith.]
especially during the last six years while the war was on. We should like especially in the lower part of -the maritimes, in Nova Scotia, and in Moncton and that vicinity, to have the Ocean Limited, running between Montreal and Halifax, made into a fast train. The train at the present time does not run a great deal faster than it did thirty years ago. The distance between Montreal and Halifax is 800 miles and, if that train made the trip in twenty or twenty-one hours, that would be about forty miles an hour, including necessary stops, which is not a great rate as railways go to-day. I will admit that speed could not be made in the winter, so that it would take a couple of hours longer. There are two other trains serving the maritimes between Montreal and Halifax, and they could well take care of the smaller stops which the Ocean Limited is now making, and they could also carry the mail and express. I should not say all mail, because it might be desirable to have the Ocean Limited carry some of the mail. All the equipment on this train has depreciated. Most of it has been in use for many years and has been rebuilt, but during the past six years it has taken an awful beating. We should like to see therefore, as soon as possible, a train made up of the latest equipment, because we feel that down there the people 800 or 600 or 500 miles away would like to travel to Montreal in as great comfort as possible. It is true that we might have to pay a little 'bit more to ride on this train, but there are sufficient people down there who would be willing, if necessary, to pay a little extra money to get to Montreal as quickly as they could, and with as great a degree of comfort as possible. There are many professional and business men down there who have to make frequent trips to Montreal and Toronto, and there are other people as well. It would be a matter of good business on the part of the railway to provide this service. To-day many people are travelling by air. If there were a crack train down there they would keep to the railways.
The minister knows that a leader always brings business. If there were a crack train on this line it would bring business to the railroad in more ways than one; in other words, it would be a leader. I have talked to the railwaymen on many occasions; and they believe, along with the public, that it will not pay to wait until a lot of traffic has left the railways and then try to get it back. Many passengers are leaving the railways and are travelling by automobile and air. A crack train would be a great thing not only

Supply

Transport
for t'he people of Nova Scotia but also for that whole section of the country. It would help to improve business for the railway.

I am glad to have my hon. friend's view, but I am sure he will realize that if he has found the equipment is not up to standard it is owing to the fact that during the war years the railway had to use anything it could get its hands on.
Why send it down to the mari times?

I may tell my hon. friend that the maritimes are not alone in that respect, but it applies to all parts of Canada. If he wishes to come into my own riding he will see that the condition of the equipment is perhaps far worse than it is in certain parts of the maritimes.

In my remarks I said that I knew the railway could not get the equipment and that it had taken a bad beating during the past six years; but as soon as equipment becomes available we should like to have it.

I was going to say to my hon. friend that perhaps he knew of the fact that some equipment w"as in process of manufacture at the present time for the Canadian National Railways and that I think some of it is being manufactured in the maritime provinces. I am hopeful that it will be possible to put some of these new coaches on that line.
With reference to the question of speed, of course that is an important factor so far as the service between Montreal and Halifax is concerned, but there is also the question of intermediate stops which comes into the picture. Sometimes it is not always possible to meet the wishes of those who want a faster train and those who want a train to stop at intermediate points.
We still want the train.
I can assure my hon. friend I am glad to have his views, and I shall ask the Canadian National Railways to explore them.

I wish to call the minister's attention to the resolution which was discussed at an earlier date of this session and which was to the effect that consideration be given to the building of a Peace River outlet. This may not be the time to discuss that matter fully, and I do not wish to reiterate what was said at that time; but I wish to impress on the minister that we want that railroad just as other parts of Canada
want railroads. The government might just as well make up its mind that it has to be built; the people of Canada have to be served.
I wish to ask the minister a question or two in, regard to the Peace River situation. First, has the government had an opportunity to give any further consideration to the matter? Second, is the minister in a position to say whether there has been any approachment by the provincial governments to the federal government for some joint action in regard to building that road? Third, does the minister know what the provincial government is proposing, and if the provincial government is going to build a line does he know which route has been selected? If the minister has any information along these lines will he be kind enough to let us know?

With reference to the second question, whether there has been any approachment by the provincial government to the federal government, I am not aware of any. I think that disposes of the other questions, save the first. With regard to that question, consideration was given to the building of a railway by the government into the Peace River district, and having regard to the reasons given during the lengthy debate which took place on the resolution and for additional reasons since apparent it was felt that this was not the time to build a railway into the Peace River district.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I wish to say a word in support of the representations made to the committee by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants. I would also add that, while the necessity of speeding up the Ocean Limited is obvious, more desirable than that is an improvement of the roadbed between Moncton and Halifax. I think the time has come to consider the question of a double track over that busy roadbed. During the war it was perhaps subject to a greater burden of traffic than any other roadbed in the dominion.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. Recently the regional headquarters of the Canadian National Railways at Moncton issued a directive the effect of which would be to prohibit the unloading of cars into freight sheds in Halifax on Sundays and holidays except in cases of emergency. The result is that, on different occasions since this directive was issued, ships which have arrived in Halifax have been delayed owing to the refusal of the railways to supply working gangs at the request of the shipping agents. This directive works a hardship not only on the longshoremen of Halifax but also on those who
Supply-Transport

are interested in the shipping activities there and who naturally want to induce as much traffic as possible to go through the port. It is quite obvious that if ships are delayed there is a tendency on the part of shipowners, shipping interests and shipping agents to divert traffic elsewhere. I ask the minister to use his influence and have this directive cancelled.

I am happy to tell the hon. gentleman that that matter has already been taken up with the management of the Canadian National Railways, but as yet I have not had a report on it. As soon as I receive it I shall be glad to apprise the hon. member of it.

I have another question or two in connection with the Peace River outlet which was raised by the hon. member for Cariboo. What is the policy of the government, to wait until the country is completely settled and producing paying quantities of freight before it is determined that the road should be built, or is its policy to build railway facilities so that the country can become settled and fully developed? That is my first question.
In the second place, surely it must be obvious to the minister and the board that the Peace River country could develop much more rapidly and do its part toward fulfilling the needs of the world for food production, and the production of minerals and other things, if the railway were not only continued on the Pacific coast, but improved from Edmonton to the Peace River district. Has any thought been given to improving the road bed and putting better equipment on that run? I have been on the road many times, and I have found that it is actually dangerous to ride on those trains from Edmonton to the Peace River. They cannot go faster than twenty miles an hour at any time; and at times when one is trying to sleep those old cars continue to rock and creak, so that sleep becomes impossible. That happens even in the winter time, and it continues as though the car were going to tip over. Surely the roadbed and the equipment ought to be improved so as to give a better type of service to the many thousands of people who are struggling up in that country to make their contribution to the economic welfare of this country and the world.
When the minister replies will he give us some assurance that something will be done as soon as possible to give the people there some encouragement? It is an empire in itself, and I am sure if the road were continued on to the coast, one way or another, and improvements made in the approach to the Peace

River, Canada will see a tremendous development throughout that whole country, and an increased production nothing short of astounding.

I do not wish to discuss the matter at great length, because I spoke at some length on this subject during the course of the debate on the resolution of the hon. member for Cariboo. Let me say briefly, however, that even among railway engineers there is a divergence of opinion as to whether a line should go into a virgin country first and then bring in the settlers, or whether settlement should be brought in and the projected line then built.
What is your policy?

The policy of the Department of Transport to a considerable extent must depend upon what the Canadian National railways-if the line in question is in the territory of that organization-advises and recommends. In this instance, the hon. member knows the Northern Alberta railways are owned jointly by the Canadian Pacific railway company and the Canadian National railways. I would not at this or at any other time attempt to tell him what the policy of another railway is or might be. I do not know what the policy of the Canadian Pacific railway company is. But I do know that there would have to be joint agreement by the railways in connection with what the hon. member seeks.
I know many of the things he has said are true, and were brought out in the committee on railways and shipping. I can only say in reply that perhaps the position he complains about is at least in some respects due to a lack of materials and equipment. The condition of the roadbeds is a matter affecting not only the Northern Alberta railways, but many other railways. I am glad the hon. member has discussed the matter in the house because, not only will it come to the attention of the Canadian Pacific Railway, through Hansard, but so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, I shall see that it is brought to their attention.

I wonder if the minister could give us any further information respecting freight rates on beets, a matter which he had under consideration during the summer. I speak not only for the beet growers in the Red River valley, but for those throughout Canada. The minister knows that the present freight rates in Canada, which are only temporary, are renewed each year to meet motor truck competition, and that there are variations in different territories.

Private Bills
To-day the farmer in the United States receives more for his beets than does the farmer in Canada. On top of that, the United States farmer enjoys a cheaper freight rate than we have in Canada. I have the schedule here, but I shall not take the time of the committee to go into it in detail. However, on the average 50-mile haul the Canadian farmer pays 1-7 cents per ton-mile, whereas the United States farmer pays only one cent. On the 100-mile haul the Canadian farmer pays T1 cent per ton-mile, while the United States farmer pays only -7 cents. The minister will realize that there is considerable difference in these rates.
I am wondering if the minister has anything to say in this connection, because the sugar beet industry has a great stabilizing influence on the economic life of the communities in *which sugar beet factories are established. They employ a great many people, and operate throughout the year.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Church for the second reading of bill No. 27, to amend the criminal code (motor cars).

subtopic: FATAL ACCIDENTS AND INJURIES FROM HIGHWAY TRAFFIC AND LEVEL CROSSINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask a question about order No. 21, resuming the adjourned debate on the motion for the second reading of this bill. This bill has not been considered at all. I gave up an hour to the government one night when I otherwise could have proceeded with it. I want to ask the minister one short question. This parliament has been. sitting now for 105 days and we have had no discussion at all of the terrible loss of life occurring in this country every week-end. There are thousands of people injured or killed in our cities, on the highways and at level crossings. The British post office stamp all mail calling attention to this danger on the highways with the slogan: "Take no chances; keep death off the road." The appalling loss of life that takes place through the motor car is almost equal to the loss of life in the great war. I hope that in the recess the government will take steps to curb the reckless and criminal negligence that people are guilty of on our highwajrs. It has been condemned by high court judges, county court judges, juries, coroners, magistrates and the public press. It is appalling to think of people being sent into the next world without one second's notice. Yet we have not found time this session to devote five minutes to this menace to life. I gladly gave up time several evenings to aid government measures, at the request of the powers that be when this bill might have been discussed. I appreciate all that the Minister of Justice has done. He has been most obliging, courteous and kind to private members, but I must urge that something be done to curb recklessness in driving motor cars in the cities and on the highways. I do not want to see the minister killed. His predecessor told me that he was .nearly knocked down when crossing the street in Ottawa. No one knows who may be next. I do not want to see the leader of our party killed or the active Minister of Reconstruction and Supply.

Criminal Code
I believe the time has come when this parliament should educate the public to the dangers and do something to curb the awful loss of life that occurs through the motor car and enforce the laws. Our legislation is defective at the present time, especially respecting hit-and-run drivers. Negligence is shown all along the line. I suggest to the minister that during the recess of parliament something should be done about this menace, a survey made and a remedy found. I should like to hear from the minister on this matter.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I shall not make a lengthy statement about this matter. We all deplore negligence on the highways, but who of us are not from time to time guilty of some negligence?
Motor traffic on the highways is a matter that is peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the local authorities, provincial and municipal. The only way in which this parliament can deal with it is under the criminal code, and under the criminal code there are very severe penalties for reckless driving. It is up to the local authorities to enforce both the criminal code and their own laws and regulations with respect to motor traffic. I know that some provincial authorities have adopted, as a rule that is obligatory upon the courts before which cases for reckless driving come, the cancellation of the driver's licence for a period. We from time to time receive applications that we should recommend to His Excellency that the term for which a licence is cancelled or suspended should be changed; but since I have occupied the office of Minister of Justice no such recommendation has been made without the assent of the minister in charge of the highways of the province in which the applicant resided, because I felt tha't it would be quite improper for any federal officer to give the right to use the highways of a province to someone who had, under the laws or regulations of the province, been deprived of that right.
I think some useful purpose can be served by a debate in this house which is reported in the newspapers and which serves to impress upon the public the necessity for everyone to exercise the greatest possible care in handling these powerful vehicles. No one a few years ago would have thought that it was possible to trust the handling of a locomotive to someone who had not had a long period of training in handling it, although the locomotive follows rigid rails and has priority over other traffic. Motor cars have not perhaps the same power as locomotives, but they travel quite as fast and it requires very
little study or training to be allowed to obtain a driver's licence. There are unfortunately many accidents. In view of the facilities with which a driver's licence is obtainable and the large numbers who have such licences, the accidents are perhaps not as. numerous as they might be. Nevertheless that is no reason why everyone should not be extremely careful.
I have only once appeared before the assizes in a criminal case. I was asked to defend a young man who had had the misfortune to be involved in an accident in which a workman had been killed. The young man was acquitted. I have not seen him for several years, but I know that at that time he felt that that accident was something which was going to darken the whole of his life. That is something, I think, which should be, more often than it is, brought to the attention of those who drive cars. No one means to kill anybody, but when it does happen it is for the one who is involved as driver a most distressing experience, and I think that is something which might be more often mentioned as an incentive to those who handle motor cars to drive them with the greatest possible degree of care. Once more, I think the hon. member intends to render and does render a service to his fellow citizens by asking that something be said about this in the House of Commons; but as to what can be done, I think the most effective action is to appeal to the deep sense of responsibility of the average citizen.

Before the house rose at six o'clock, the hon. member for Selkirk raised a point about freight rates on sugar beets, and referred to a discrimination between the Canadian rate as opposed to the United States rate. At the time I was not able to give him an answer, because there are some forty thousand tariff items which are handled by the board of transport commissioners. The hon. gentleman will understand that the Department of Transport as such has no jurisdiction over tariff rates, that that is a matter which is under the board of transport commissioners. The practice is for the railway to file a tariff with the board, who in turn post the tariff up in the locality where it is to apply, and if there is any objection to it a complaint can be made to the board. It may well be that in the case mentioned by the hon. gentleman the shippers have made representations to the railways, but I have inquired of the board of transport commissioners and I am informed by them that no complaint covering this particular tariff item on sugar beets has been made to them. So the best advice I can give my hon. friend is this, that if the shippers are not able to obtain satisfaction from their railways they can always appeal to the board of transport commissioners, who will adjudicate upon it.

During the budget debate I introduced the subject of an application on the part of the Nova Scotia government to the national harbours board with respect to the establishment of a flour mill or the securing of a site. This has been a matter of contro-very for some time between the minister of industry in the Nova Scotia government and the federal government. Later in the debate, the Minister of Transport made quite a lengthy statement and went into considerable detail to offset what the minister of industry in the Nova Scotia government had said. Now, in a press dispatch on July 17-and I want the minister to clear this matter up because it is of some importance in Nova Scotia-the minister of industry of Nova Scotia, commenting on what the Minister of Transport had said here in the budget debate with reference to that matter, issued the following statement, upon which the minister may wish to comment during his estimates:

Mr. Connolly said:	"Mr. Chevrier is undoubtedly not familiar with all the facts. This is understandable in view of the fact that his predecessor, J. E. Michaud, was Minister of Transport when these negotiations were carried on. No alternative site was ever suggested by the national harbours board. On the contrary, we suggested an alternative site immediately behind pier 23, which was rejected by the national harbours board. They turned it down because, they said, there was not sufficient space to erect our plant there and because such a plant would interfere with the grain conveyers. It is absolutely incorrect that an engineer of the harbours board did survej this area for an alternative site. He was here part of one day, came in to see me and told me that he did not have the time to make a survey. The fact is that pier 25 was immobilized last year and used only for storage purposes and it was almost entirely inactive."
I am not questioning the merits or demerits of Mr. Connolly's statement or the statement of the Minister of Transport, but-
You would just like a little argument, would you?

-I think it is of some importance to the people of Nova Scotia to have the matter clarified in their minds. If the Nova Scotia government desired to establish an industry which, although not very big, would employ some people and provide something we have not at the present time, and they were blocked by some federal commission or because of laxity on the part of those in authority, which is the accusation made by the minister of industry of Nova Scotia- and do not forget that he is a Liberal minister in a Liberal government, so that it is a family quarrel-I am merely trying to referee it to see that somebody gets fair play; but I am not arguing this statement with the minister; I am simply bringing it to his attention-he may not have read it-so that he may be able to put the facts on the record as they really are and enlighten the people of Nova Scotia. You may be running an election down there again and we want to have the record straight.
I would also ask the minister if he would be good enough, when he has time and before the estimates are disposed of, to give us some indication as to how far the Canso project has developed. I believe the railway is connected with the project and there is talk of rerouting the road through Guysborough county. If he has anything further to say on the subject I shall be pleased to read it in Hansard to-morrow. I am sorry I cannot stay for his other estimates, but there are odds and ends that

have to be taken care of somewhere else and I am going to try to make some contribution towards settling the steel dispute. I think we shall be busy for the rest of the evening. I wish to thank the hon. member for Kamloops for his courtesy in allowing me the floor.

Perhaps I had better reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He refers to a statement made by Hon. Mr. Connolly, minister of industry and publicity in the Nova Scotia government. I have looked at the statement and, frankly, there is not a great deal of difference between us with the exception perhaps of two things. I can find in the statement nothing that disagrees greatly with what I said in my speech on the budget, when I believe I went into the matter of the flour mill at the port of Halifax at length on that occasion. I do not want to go into it again to-night, but I repeat that nothing in the statement made by Mr. Connolly disagrees very much with what I said. The only two points with which I can possibly take issue, are first, the statement reported in the Halifax Chronicle as follows:
No alternative site was ever suggested by the national harbours board.
The answer to that statement is that two alternative sites were suggested by the engineer of the board who went down to make the investigation. The flour mill people and the engineer from Port Arthur or Fort William insisted that it should be pier 23 or nothing else. As the hon. gentleman knows, pier 23 is a facility of the national harbours board, and it was impossible for the board to immobilize that facility. There were, however, other alternative sites,
With reference to the other part of the statement, I quote:	*
It is absolutely incorrect that an engineer of the national harbours board did survey this area for an alternative site. He was here part of one day, came in to see me and told me that he did not have the time to make a survey.
The answer to that is that the engineer is Mr. Russell Yuill, then an engineer of the national harbours board, now port manager at the port of Saint John, and he positively states that he was in Halifax for three days and did make a survey.
With reference to Canso, on June 4 I gave the hon. member for Cape Breton South a fairly complete statement on the project. I have not a great deal to add to that, save to say that since that time a contract has been given for the borings to J. P. Porter and Sons; they have succeeded in boring three holes, and the work is still progressing.
So far as the railway is concerned, I should not like to say more than this, that when I discussed it last year I told the house there were several proposals in view, one having to do with relocation of a low-grade line of railway from Sunnybrae to connect with the Antigonish and Mulgrave line, but that it depended on the nature of the project over the gut of Canso, and that so far as these proposals were concerned, they would be carefully considered by the department. I said that the question of the railway would depend on which of these three or four proposals was finally adopted by the department. I do not think I can say more than that.
Thank you very much.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Kamloops intimated the other night that he would like to discuss highways at this time. On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I am not aware, although I have tried to find out, that there is a rule which lays it down that there must be a particular estimate in the department which is under discussion before a member can raise a certain point. It has been the custom-and I believe this is unquestionable-that on the first item, departmental administration, members are permitted a certain latitude to discuss general matters in connection with the department. Admittedly, a trans-Canada highway is not a subject of federal expenditure and, therefore, not at the moment a matter in respect of which the government has a policy. The purpose of my remarks, however, is to suggest that the dominion government should have a highway policy and should give serious consideration to the immediate development of at least one decent trans-Canada highway in order to promote the progress and development of this country. I would point out that a good many years ago, to be exact, in 1912 and 1913, a bill was introduced by the then

minister of railways -and canals to provide for a federal highway programme and for federal assistance to the provinces in developing their own roads. That is why I chose this department upon which to make my remarks.

That was federal assistance to the provinces in respect, I presume, of relief. Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: It seems that the constituency which I represent is singularly
unfortunate in that it has two lines of railway

which are incomplete at the present time. I should now like to draw attention to the second one, which was started from St. Walburg to Beaver River or Cold Lake. The roadbed was actually completed for some miles and ties were laid down. Afterwards they were moved and since that time the roadbed has been used as a highway. The people in that district are suffering a hardship because of the failure to complete that line and at times they are under a definite handicap. Will the minister be good enough to make a statement or tell us just what the situation is concerning that particular railway? At a time when foodstuffs are so important the farmers in our country should be encouraged and helped in every possible way to produce as much as they possibly can. Instead of that, because they have not a railway completed, they are, as I say, handicapped in their production. I shall be glad if I can have a statement concerning that particular line.

The gap to which my hon. friend refers, namely, that between St. Walburg and Bonnyville is a much more considerable one than that which he discussed before the six o'clock recess. It is 125-9 miles in length. It has been given careful consideration by the Canadian National Railways. In fact the Canadian National Railways is not at all disposed against it; all to the contrary, if anything.
The portion between Bonnyville and Beaver River has been started in part. I believe the rails have been laid down, but strong representations have been made for a .change in the course of the line from the St. Walburg end. In other words, it has been suggested that a line might be built east of the present location as a possible alternative route. That has necessitated a further consideration by way of survey. The Canadian National Railways are careful about the manner in which they proceed. After having obtained a survey for an area and then representations having been made that the area should not be served but that the line should be diverted to take up another route such as has been the case here, the railways go into the financial as well as the traffic possibilities. So far as the St. Walburg-Bonnyville line is concerned, all I can say to my hon. friend at the moment is that, in view of the representations made for the change of the location between St. Walburg and Loon Lake, it would be necessary to have a further survey made of that portion. to tell my hon. friend, but I know the Canadian National Railways have the matter actively before them.

the board of railway commissioners should make a study of the situation accordingly as represented.
During the war, aids to navigation on the great lakes were not what they should be. A survey in this connection should be made throughout the great lakes, because it would seem that most of the money for the use of the department is spent on the gulf and river St. Lawrence, but very little of it on the great lakes for aids to navigation on the upper lakes, where there is siueh a heavy tonnage. It is of interest to know that the tonnage on the great lakes and the Welland canal is equal to that of the Panama canal. I should hope that something might be done to aid some of the boat captains and their crews with better labour conditions on the ships. I know, when I was chairman of the harbour board in Toronto, and head of the city, we had to establish a long row of white hydro lights at the eastern entrance of Toronto harbour, because the captains of the lake boats could not make the port in rough [DOT]weather. In fact there was rough weather tliere; accidents occurred and some few were drowned on the lakes in the late fall. When the minister's estimates are considered I hope a study will be made of aids to navigation on the great lakes with the fall storms. I know that many of the lights are too low, and should be elevated.
There are. three other items to which I should refer, the first of which is life saving for which an amount of $44,430 is set aside in these estimates. I wish to protest against what the harbour board of Toronto has had to do in connection with life saving. In that city we have spent far more than this $44,000 on this service there alone; and the lifesaving crew from that city at times has to go to Georgian bay, Muskoka, Lake Simcoe, New Ontario, the St. Lawrence river and to the bay of Quinte. Telephone calls come in constantly for the services of the Toronto lifesaving crew to recover dirownings.
I do not know what would happen if a steamer were to be wrecked on the lake or in the Niagara river at the present time. I know that during the first great war the Cayuga, the old Chippawa and the Corona had great difficulty at times in making harbour. I can remember when the present Minister of National Defence in the first world war was serving with the McGill battery over there, and it was one of those boats that carried him over there. The same is true of His Gracious Majesty, the present King, who happened to be on one of those boats, the Chippawa, which was scarcely able to make
[Mr. Church.l
port because of bad weather and heavy seas. That was the occasion of his first visit as a navel cadet to Niagara in 1913.
It is the duty of the department to save the lives of passengers on ships, and to guard against drownings on the great lakes. Toronto has had to d'o this all over Ontario, and even to New Ontario. At the present time they simply telephone to Toronto for the life savers from that city, and Toronto gets nothing for it. This is a heavy burden on the taxpayers of that city and I hope something will be done to relieve them of some of the burden, or pay half the cost to our city, which is over $55,000 a year.
Then, I have great respect for the steamboat inspectors, all good men, who' make inspections of hulls, boilers, plates, engines and that sort of thing. I wish to point out, however, that they are taking great chances at the present time. The department has built up a splendid business at Port Dalhousie-not "Port Dall-howsie", as the captains used to call it. It has been called all kinds of names. But you have built up a splendid business there, the Niagara, St. Catharines, C.N.R. subsidiary. The department operates the Dalhousie City- and also that old tub, the Northumberland which thirty years ago was not good enough for the strait of Northumberland. Prince Edward Island. But they sent it up to our town, and it is still running. I am afraid there will be accidents on it, and a new ship is wanted for next year. I travelled on it once or twice to the Canadian Henley, but I would never risk my life on it again. It is time some of the large amount of money the government is making out of these subsidiaries in the Niagara district was spent on a new ship. I know, too, that there was a request for a car ferry at Cobourg, which ran for a few days. A bumper business awaits it in the Niagara peninsula.
I have concluded about all I should like to say on these estimates. The signals service is all wrong. The department has spent large sums of money in air and rail services. Some of the work done has been very good. We realize that the radio division is necessary, although some of the ships are not equipped with radio. There is radio equipment on some of the passenger boats on the great lakes, and to Niagara and Port Dalhousie, but it is time the radio service was extended and improved, and more aids given to steamboat captains on the upper lakes in the late fall in stormy weather.
There is very heavy revenue from the traffic in the Welland canal, and because of that I hope better working conditions will

Supply-Transport
be provided for canal workers. I shall not refer to all the items to-night, 'because I do not wish to delay the passage of the estimates. I would hope, however, that a further study would be made by the minister, and that in doing so he will not forget the great lakes, where the main tonnage is found. He should not forget, either, that the marine service on those lakes acts as a regulator of freight rates for six months of the year. In the old days boats used to come in to Toronto from Col-borne, Brighton, Cobourg, Port Hope and Oshawa. But the traffic on the roads has eliminated those boats.
The marine service in the Niagara district is the most important. New boats are needed. I should hope the boats would be enlarged and the system extended. Great numbers of people now like to travel by water in the summer months, and the minister would do well to study this question during the recess of parliament.
I shall delay the committee for only a moment.
Hear, hear.

I am in agreement with that, myself. I should like to place upon the record something which I believe will be pleasing to the ears of hon. members, and which will also be informative.
During the last session of parliament other hon. members joined me in expressing our interest in the railway workers of Canada. At that time, we placed on record our humble tribute to the magnificent job done by the railway companies and their employees during the war, and I should like to renew my tribute this evening.
Before being called to the international conference overseas last fall, I received a message from the Canadian automotive transport association, which is a federation of provincial motor transport organizations. One of the pleasing parts of that communication from this entirely different type of transportation organization was that, in the very first line, they said that they took their hats off to the job the railways of Canada had done during the war. This expression prompted me to make inquiries respecting the work done by the automotive transport organization, because I thought the splendid spirit which this organization of rubber-tired transport workers had shown toward the railways should be reciprocated, if possible.
Looking into their wartime activities, I found that no less than 32,000 men, or forty-five per cent of this group of for-hire interurban carriers enlisted during the war for
wartime duties overseas and in Canada. The job which they did in carrying wartime express and freight for Canada could be described as nothing short of spectacular.
In closing my brief remarks, I should also like to pay a tribute to the noble work done by those who carried passengers in rubber-tired' vehicles. During 1939 these passenger coaches and buses of Canada carried a total- I think this will be rather interesting to the committee because it is not always easy to get statistics of rubber-tired traffic-of 16,600,000 passengers in 1,500 vehicles. In 1944, the second to the last year of the war, they carried 73,375,316 passengers in 2,562 vehicles. The total mileage in 1939 was 46,000,000 miles as against 73,000,000 miles in 1944. That gives some indication of the importance of this sister method of passenger transportation. Its achievements can appropriately be set alongside the magnificent job done by the railroads to help Canada's war effort achieve its gigantic objective.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on behalf of the people who have been petitioning the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Minister of Transport and different governments during the past fifteen years to have a line of railway known as the Valmarie-Mankota gap completed. The distance between these two points is thirty-seven miles. This country has been settled for thirty-five years, and about twenty-three years ago the C.P.R. started to build a branch line from Assiniboia to Notukeu, leaving a gap of thirty-seven miles unbuilt. This gap has occasioned great hardship and losses on the sale of products and has retarded development for many years. Several years ago the Assiniboia board of trade arranged a meeting with Mr. D. C. Coleman, then president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. At that meeting two questions were asked Mr. Coleman, the first one being:
Can we be sure that the road will be completed, as it has been rumoured that it might swing north from Mankota and not connect with Yalmarie?
Mr. Coleman's reply was that it was mere rumour, that the road would be connected with Valmarie. The next question was:
When could the job be expected to be completed?
To which Mr. Coleman replied:
I can promise you this, that when the finances of the company are such that we can take on a building programme, that will be one of the first jobs taken on.
It is understood that the Canadian Pacific has set aside large sums of tax-free money for post-war construction, and the people feel

Supply-Transport
that the government should take steps to see that these branch lines are completed by the railroad. Surely people who have been waiting all these years, deserve to be considered, as wed as the Canadian Pacific shareholders. This uncompleted gap has put the brakes on production and has added to the costs of the producers. The extra cost of hauling grain by truck is from eight to ten cents a bushel and shipping cream is out of the question. You must either make a 37-mile trip by truck to the north line or else wait for the train which makes only one trip a week. Stock shipped to Moose Jaw from Valmarie is on the train two days and has to be unloaded and fed on the way. When they leave Valmarie they go to Notukeu; then, they go back to Shaunavon in the one day, and they are just thirty-five miles north from where they started.
There are twenty-three shipping points on this branch line and, according to information from the pool, a total of five and a half million bushels of grain has been shipped out from these points in one year, to say nothing about the live stock, coal and other tilings that are shipped in. I want to say here that if the Weyburn-Lethbridge Canadian Pacific line were a Canadian National line there would be no question about this gap being filled in. As things stand now, the produce is hauled to another shipping point on the Canadian Pacific line to the north. They get it all anyway. I should like to quote from a letter written by Mr. W. M. Neal, vice-president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as follows:
When construction of the lines which now terminate at Valmarie and Mankota was commenced, it was anticipated that the development along the projected route would progress at a rate which would justify this company in continuing, long ere this, construction from each end until both lines met. Unfortunately, our hopes in this respect were disappointed, partially no doubt as a result of the severe drought of the 1930's. The second great war which began in September, 1939, has undoubtedly since then had its effect in retarding this long hoped for development. At more or less regular intervals requests have been received that we proceed with this work on the ground that the absence of the completed railway imposes a hardship upon the people living within the area unserved directly by a railway, and also those on the line west of Valmarie. We fully appreciate their position and their consequent desire for the completion of that line. We find ourselves looking to the future in a position where we cannot afford to expend large amounts of capital without feeling assured of a reasonable return on the investment.
This makes it quite plain that the road was built with one purpose in view, money, not to serve the people. The letter continues:
[Mr. McCuaig.l
I am sure it is apparent to you that . . . with the higher price of coal and other commodities we must now, with decreasing traffic, avoid commitments which do not indicate their, ability to pay their way and show a return on the capital expended.
From the foregoing it would appear that the Canadian Pacific has no intention of completing this line. In my opinion the time has come when the government will have to take decisive steps to see that the people living along these uncompleted lines get the much needed transportation facilities. Service to and welfare of the people should be the first consideration. The Canadian Pacific has b^en given many concessions and privileges; and I think it is the bounden duty of the government, as the parent of the nation, to see that along with these concessions and privileges there goes some responsibility. The people trust that the Minister of Transport and the government will see that this line is built. I would ask the minister to make a statement to the committee as to what is to be done about these uncompleted branch lines. Present conditions are working a hardship on the people. According to a letter that I have received, a mass meeting was held in Valmarie last week demanding action, and the returned men did not take very kindly to the treatment they are receiving. They went overseas to fight for a Canada fit to live in, not to come back to live in hardships. I trust that the government will do something about this matter.

The hon. member asks for a statement. I will give him one very briefly. I am sure he will understand at once that the line to which he refers is in an entirely different category from what the hon. member for North Battleford urged with reference to the gap at Bonnyville-St. Walburg and Heinsburg-Frenchman Butte. Those two gaps to which the hon. member referred are in the territory of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian National Railways is responsible to parliament through the Minister of Transport, but not so with reference to the line to which the hon. member for Maple Creek has referred. The Minister of Transport has no power to order the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to build a branch line or to fill any gap. The Canadian Pacific is a private company and any representations which the hon. gentleman has to make in regard to it should be directed to that corporation. However, I shall be glad to send a copy of. Hansard containing my hon. friend's remarks to the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company so that he will be able to take under advisement what my hon. friend has said.

When the hon. member for North Battleford spoke, he stated he had the misfortune to have two unfinished branch lines in his constituency. I have the misfortune to have five. However, there are just two of these that I am concerned with. There is the line from Scapa to Hemaruka and the line from Bulwark to Airways and Bodo. In the line from Scapa to Hemaruka there is a gap of twenty-four miles from Spondin to Hemaruka which has never been ballasted.

Supply-Transport
Steels were laid, and in the early days a number of freight trains were run. But the right of way was never fenced, and therefore the trainmen had to stop and open and shut the gates every time they went through a farmer's land. These trains ran for a number of years, and there is a strong feeling throughout that area that that gap of twenty-four miles should be ballasted. I realize that it would cost a good deal of money to complete it. I drew this matter to the minister's attention some months ago when I received a petition from residents in that area. I pointed out to the minister at that time that, while it might have been uneconomic in the past to run trains through that district, I believe the whole picture is changing, because the Red Deer diversion scheme is being put through, and if the land is irrigated, no doubt the amount of business will be increased considerably. This year the government has appropriated $115,000 to check the engineering details of the Red Deer diversion scheme, and the Minister of Agriculture stated in the house this year that in all probability tenders would be let and the scheme would be proceeded with. Business will then increase and there will be a real need for this line to be completed. Of course this line is on the Canadian National Railways.
The other line is one from Bulwark to Airways and Bodo. There is no break between Airways and Bodo, and the amount of business has increased in that area considerably during the past few years. This matter I also brought to the attention of the minister along with the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Camrose, and a petition was presented by me from these people. Can the minister give us any information as to whether the picture as far as the Scapa-Hemaruka line has changed since last year?

I am afraid I cannot give the hon. member much information with reference to the Scapa-Hemaruka line, because, while I remember the representations that were made by himself and, I think, one or two of his colleagues at the time, what I did was to ask for a report on it, but I have not obtained one from the railways. With reference to the Bulwark-Airways line, that is a line which is some 26-9 miles in length; it serves an agricultural country, and some work was done on it under the 1929-32 branch line construction programme. But, as the hon. gentleman knows, there is no such programme before the house, and I am not in a position to tell him whether there will be one in the future, certainly not in the immediate future. But at the time that a survey was made of the Bulwark-Airways line it was thought that, in view of the expen-63260-312
diture required to complete the gap, the railway would not be justified in completing the line. I do not know the date of this survey, but I think it was 1945. There may be some change in the position since then. I should be glad to explore it and tell my hon. friend what the result is.
I should like the minister to do that, because there has been quite an improvement in that area in the past few years.

Last session this question of unfinished branch lines was discussed, and I am sorry that I was not in the house this evening when the minister made a statement in connection with the Heinsburg-Frenchman Butte line. This is the second session now that these matters have been brought to the attention of the house and the question has been considered of lines being started and never finished. We have to remember that when these lines are started they are started with the idea of bringing in settlers, and those settlers go there under the promise that they will have railway service. It seems to me that the railways have a responsibility. The situation is this. The line which has been referred to by the hon. member for Maple Creek is a Canadian Pacific branch line and we have no jurisdiction over the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but we can understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company,-not being a publicly owned organization, is not likely to build branch lines unless it can see a profit in them. But that railway does do something else. It goes into districts where we have our own Canadian National line, and I am sure they have even built these branch lines with the idea of robbing our own system. I am perfectly sure they do that even though they will lose money on it.
Last session and the session before, and in fact since 1928, these two branch lines that were discussed by the hon. member for North Battleford were started, and a promise was given the people there. These people have been doing that long haul all these years, not only having to haul produce long distances but having to pay a high backhaul, an extra charge they should not have to pay. We shall soon have to have a showdown in this country on the question of a national railway policy. There must be a solution to the railway problem and we must answer the question whether we are going to give our people the sendee they require. It is the duty of the government to see that the people are serviced by railways and the only solution is to have one railway system. If we had just one railway system we would do away

Supply-Transport

with a tremendous amount of duplication. In some cases where the branch line might not quite balance, but might nearly do so, that line would be more likely to be completed. As it is, however, under the present system, with one private line having been allowed by past governments to build branch lines to rob our own national system, the situation is absolutely wrong, and I want the minister to answer this question. How does a private railway in Canada obtain franchises to go in and cut in on the business that should really go to our own railway?

On the subject of the Heinsburg-Frenchman Butte line, I dealt with that in answer to another hon. member and I do not think I can be expected to deal with it again.
With reference to the second part of my hon. friend's remarks, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company obtains charters to build branch lines in the same manner as the Canadian National. It comes to parliament for them; the matter is referred to a committee, and parliament approves or disapproves. Any lines which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has obtained were obtained in that manner.
The Railway Act contains a provision covering the subject, and whether or not there is competition between the two railways, the fact is that an act was passed some years ago, the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Railway Act, in which it was certainly the intention of parliament that the two railways should cooperate. They have done so to a large extent on the Northern Alberta railways and in certain hotels, and I believe there has been a disposition on the part of the railways to meet the requirements of that act and to cooperate under its provisions.
But they are not finishing branch lines.
As I told the hon. member for Maple Creek, there is little that I as Minister of Transport can do to direct or force them to complete the lines.
That is a situation that I wrould correct by nationalizing all the lines in Canada.

Under the heading "canal service", the estimates contain five items providing for an expenditure of $3,024,200 for the administration, maintenance and improvement of canals. There are no canals in New Brunswick, and consequently I do not believe that any part of this amount will be spent in New Brunswick or, in fact, in any part of the maritime provinces. Although

there are no canals in New Brunswick or in the maritimes, or almost none, it does not follow that there should not be a canal. A canal is needed to connect Northumberland strait with the bay of Fundy, and it should be 'built if, taking a long range view of the situation, it would be economically practical to build it.
This canal would cross the narrow, sandy, low-lying strip of land known as the isthmus of Chignecto, which is something less than twenty miles wide. There are three possible routes that have been suggested, none of which would involve any large amount of rock cutting or other expensive work. Each of the three proposed routes makes use of the northern or Northumberland strait end of the Tignish river, which flows into Bale Verte. At the southern or Bay of Fundy end, there are three existing channels at the present time, the Aulac river, Missaquash river and La Blanche river, any one of which could be connected with the Tignish. This canal, I am informed, was promised the people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia at the time of confederation. The first paragraph of an editorial that appeared in the Telegraph-Journal' of Saint John of November 27, last year, reads:
The pledge that a canal would he cut across the isthmus of Chignecto was one of the inducements which led the Atlantic provinces into confederation. Had it been kept, our economic story would have been different and happier. The advantages of cheap water transportation would have encouraged the development of our natural resources and given this region a larger and more prosperous population. But the province has been scandalously ignored and scorned by successive generations of politicians-to the great disadvantage of our trade and commerce.
The canal, if built, would cut down shipping distances between the St. Lawrence river and the eastern coast ports along the bay of Fundy and the United States. At present, to get from the bay of Fundy to Northumberland strait or any port on the gulf of St. Lawrence by water, it is necessary to travel around almost the whole coast or a great part of the coast of Nova Scotia via the gulf of Canso. A water trip from Saint John to Shediac in New Brunswick now covers a distance of about six hundred miles. The same trip through the proposed canal would be little more than one hundred miles in length, or a saving of five hundred miles. The distance between Saint John and Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, would be cut down from 609 miles to 179 miles, or a saving of 430 miles; the distance from Saint John to Campobello, from 830 miles to about 400 miles; from Saint John to Montreal, from 1,323 miles to about 945 miles. Savings

would be made on all trips by water from any St. 'Lawrence or great lakes port to any city on the eastern coast of the maritimes or the United States to South America.
Would the hon. member give us the saving that would be made from Montreal to Halifax?
From Montreal to Halifax? I am speaking of from Saint John to Montreal. The present distance is 1,323 miles.
The hon. member said any port on the Atlantic.
I said the distance from Saint John to Montreal by water is 1,323 miles. If the canal were built the distance would be 945 miles.

The hon. member ought to stick to the facts.

I am sticking to the facts.
No public work will assist in developing our resources in this part of Canada more than the Chignecto canal; no public work would create more jobs during the construction period or, I believe, for all time.
Surveys of the proposed canal have been made from time to time; at least half a dozen have been made, and I have read that in each case it was reported that the project was worthy of being carried through, though perhaps not immediately. The effect of the report of the commission, which was held in 1931, was that the expense could not be justified during the depression. Perhaps we now have a change of view as to what we should do during depression times. The people of the maritimes, particularly of New Brunswick, would like to see this work started. It would' create new industries; it Would provide new jobs; it would make the maritimes more prosperous. To quote again from the article in the Telegraph-Journal to which I referred a moment ago:
Nothing would develop our resources more in this part of Canada than the Chignecto canal; nothing would create more jobs, both through the construction period and for all time.
Since the last session of parliament have any further steps been taken by the government to inquire into the possibilities of undertaking this work?	.

The hon. member has referred to a question which is of a perennial nature. I think that every time the estimates 63260-3121
of the Minister of Transport are up there is a demand for the building of the Chignecto canal. There have been a number of surveys and reports made on the project, some of them dating as far back at 1822. The last one was made in 1931. Since I expected that there would be a question or a more or less lengthy debate on this matter, I brought the last report with me which was made in 1931, as I said before, by Arthur Surveyer, David W. Robb and John F. Sowards. The conclusion may be summarized briefly as follows, that from, the point of view of the local economic advantage the commission failed to see wha-t benefit it would be to the districts concerned to provide, at such great cost, a navigation facility which would intensify competition in the locality served rather than lessen it. The commission also found that the canal would have no bearing whatever upon the Canada-West Indies trade. The gravamen of the report can be found in this statement:
Having regard to transport facilities already available in the maritime area as a whole, we cannot see where any interest would suffer were the Chignecto canal project to be permitted to stand in abeyance until it can be further examined in the light of future developments in Canada's economic situation.
I can say to the hon. gentleman that, since the matter was brought up in the house last year, there have been no further submissions or reports on it. It may or may not come within the reconstruction programme. My hon. friend knows there are certain projects which have been recommended to the Department of Reconstruction. I am not aware that this one has.

The hon. member for The Battlefords mentioned the matter of the propriety of building certain lines of railways. For instance, this morning we were considering a new line. Would the building of that line of railway be considered by the board of transport commissioners?

No, not until after the line is built. After it is built it automatically comes under their jurisdiction. I presume my hon. friend has in mind the rates on pulp which we were discussing this morning. I was going to say that after the line has been built the railway must file its rates with the board. If it is not a satisfactory rate to -the shippers there can be objection to it.
