May I call the minister's attention to the poor train service on the Canadian National Railways between Calgary and Edmonton? That line has operated since 1911, and runs through one of the finest farming districts in western Canada. There used to be a daily service-I am not so sure that there were not two trains each day-but for a number of years now there has been only a train every other day. That is poor service. It is curious to note that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company runs three trains each day, including Sundays, between Calgary and Edmonton, through Red Deer.
The Canadian National Railways, running between Calgary and Edmonton, through Camrose and Mirror, has only one train every other day, which works a great hardship upon the people in that area. For instance, if they want to go to Edmonton and wish to travel on a Tuesday they would not arrive until late in the evening, and would have either to come home early the next morning, preventing their doing any business, or wait until the Friday before returning. This means a stay of two days in Edmonton or Calgary, as the case may be.
There are many complaints about this and I would ask the minister to look into the matter. It is a very poor service, and there is no reason for it that I can see. It is one of the best farming districts in western Canada.
Comparison was made this evening between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway. I can say only this, that if you ever travelled over those two lines you would decide that the Canadian National Railways service between Calgary and Edmonton is a poor advertisement for public ownership of railways.

I am pleased to have these representations from the hon. member. This is the first complaint made to me personally respecting the service between Calgary and Edmonton. I shall be glad to bring it to the attention of the Canadian National Railways officials.

I should like to refer to the fences along the Canadian Pacific railway right of way south of Assiniboia, Saskatchewan, from
Lisieux to Rockglen and west to Killdeer. I have considerable information here on my desk, among which is a letter from Peter Lode of Lisieux. I thought I might read from it those parts which set out clearly the point in question. Mr. Lode had one of his cattle beasts killed on the Canadian Pacific railway tracks. His letter states that the fences were down, that the railway company was not maintaining those fences as they should be maintained, and that for that reason the steer got on the tracks. His letter states in part:
I asked the board of transport commissioners to send an inspector out here to inspect the dilapidated fence and gates on the C.P.R. from Lisieux to Killdeer. On September 18, 1945, engineer Mr. Parks, members of the B.T.C. and three C.P.R. officials, assistant superintendent Mr. Jones of Moose Jaw, engineer Mr. Clarke of Moose Jaw, and road boss Mr. Ironrud of Assiniboia . . .
He states he followed them along the railroad track when they were making the inspection. Apparently following that they made a report to the board of transport commissioners, a copy of which was sent to Mr. Lode. In that connection Mr. Lode said this:
When I received the report from the B.T.C. I showed the report to my neighbours. They were all flabbergasted, so my neighbours suggested we take pictures of the fence and gates. Mr. Spagrud, Mr. Bjorenson and myself live between mile posts 3 and 6 along the Killdeer branch.
Then he goes on to say that they took a number of pictures. In his letter he says-he has a complaint to register against the-board of transport commissioners, because-they should protect individuals to see that, they do not suffer loss on account of neglect on the part of the railway company.
I have here a petition, not in required form, for tabling, -but the -recital of which states this:
We the undersigned residents of the above districts, hereby make the following statement:
That to our personal knowledge and experience, we say, that the C.P.R. right of way fences from the townsite of Lisieux, to Rockglen, and from Rockglen west to Killdeer, are not kept in proper repair, and that live stock can, and does get through in and on to the tracks and that we have been forced at different times to repair the C.P.R. fences ourselves, in order to keep our cattle and horses from entering on to the C.P.R. railway tracks.

Could the minister give us an explanation of the general policy of the Department of Transport with regard to the acquisition and disposal of airports throughout Canada?

This afternoon, when the hon. member for Colchester-Hants was speaking, he said that he w'as not going to deal with freight rates. Quite a smile lit up .the face of the minister. I hope that when I announce my subject that smile will broaden. I want to make a few remarks with reference to the board of transport commissioners and their administration of transportation rates in Prince Edward Island. I want to bring this to the attention of the committee and the minister.
As hon. members know, it has always been difficult for me to put my questions and to have them answered., and I find it still harder to get them implemented. However, I was sent here by the constituency of Queens to put our problems before the minister and before this committee. The problem that I intend to deal with in connection with the board of transport commissioners is in reference to truck rates, et cetera, on our feriy. There has been a continuous fight over this matter for some time. Our motto is parva sub. ingenti, the small under the great, and we

must keep up that fight for our rights. Because of our geographical position, I sometimes think our province does not get its rights as compared with the other provinces of Canada.
When we have to fight so hard for these I am reminded of a slogan which was coined by a farmer and afterwards borrowed by one of the great writers. This farmer was watching a bulldog pup in deadly combat with a great Dane dog. Finally the bulldog pup triumphed and then the farmer coined this saying:	"It
isn't the size of the dog in the fight that counts, but the size of the fight in the dog that wins." We must live up to that motto of ours, parva sub ingenti.
On July 8-and this brings me to my subject-I asked a question with reference to transportation. I directed this question to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport. The Prime Minister passed the question on .to the Minister of Transport. My question was:
Under what or by whose authority is the board of transport commissioners to hold a meeting in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, on July 17 next, regarding truck freight rates on the Borden-Tormentine ferry?
The Minister of Transport replied as follows:
. . . any individual or group of individuals may make application to the board of transport commissioners to have rates revised.
The minister promised to give a more definite answer later on. At that time I protested at the holding of a transport board meeting	in	Charlottetown. The	Speaker
would not allow me to debate the subject or even to give my reasons for protesting, so that I now take this opportunity to do so. The Speaker ruled me out of order on that day, but on the following day the minister made this statement:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Queens	(Mr.	McLure) asked the	following
question:
Under what or by whose authority is the board of transport commissioners to hold a meeting	in	Charlottetown,	Prince	Edward
Island, on July 17 next, regarding truck freight rates on the Borden-Tormentine ferry?

I still say, as I have said time and time before in this house, that that is not a correct answer.	I should like to	refer briefly to
Hansard of December 17, 1945, at pages 3685 and 3686. I shall not read it all, but I should like to refer to the points dealing directly with this question. I quote:
Why should they

Let me refer now to the protest I made on July 8 and my reasons for same. First, it is not within the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners to determine whether or not there has been a fulfilment of the terms of confederation between Prince Edward Island and the dominion as entered into in 1873. Second, under the British North America Act the dominion parliament and it alone, through its Minister of Transport of the government, has the exclusive authority over all matters such as rates, freight rates, et cetera, on ferries between a province and any British or foreign country, or between any two provinces (see section 91 subsection 13 of the British North America Act). On the two mentioned points I made my protest but did not get it on the record at that time.
Under these two points what could the board of transport commissioners do about setting or revising rates when they went to Charlottetown? It was and is entirely outside the jurisdiction of the board of transport. The ferries must be treated as national highways under the pact of 1873.
Furthermore, there is nothing in the Railway Act which gives the board of transport commissioners the jurisdiction to determine rates, charges, et cetera, on an interprovincial ferry which the railway does not own, does not charter, or does not maintain. I want to emphasize that-which the railway does not own, does not charter, or does not maintain.
Before submitting further proof for my protest, let me again quote the transportation terms of 1873 between my province and the dominion. The dominion gave a guarantee to Prince Edward Island'-and here is the guarantee:
To assume and defray all the charges for efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, et cetera.
And further:
Such other charges as may be incident to, and connected with the services which by the British North America Act, 1867, appertain to the general government, and as are or may be allowed to other provinces.
Let me further endeavour to convince the Minister of Transport that he is the man with the power, or I might say to him as regards ourselves that he is the "Ingenti".
The board of transport commissioners held their hearings in Charlottetown on July 17 and 18 last and may have reported to the minister. I do not know. But I have seen a full report of their hearings.
I may tell my hon. friend that I have not.
I can supply the minister with a verbatim report.
I shall be glad to see it.

Evidently my protest of their jurisdiction came before the meeting, either directly or indirectly, and how did they consider it? Here is what they said with regard to it. Mr. A. K. Dysart, Montreal, was legal counsel representing the Canadian National Railways, and here is what he said under examination:
This matter (the terms of confederation) was an issue between the province and the dominion over which the transport commission had no jurisdiction.
Chief Commissioner J. A. Cross, K.C., agreed with the legal counsel Mr. Dysart, and here is what he said.:
There seems to be a good deal involved outside of our sphere. So far as we are concerned, we are going to confine ourselves to our own jurisdiction under the Railway Act, possibly supplemented by the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
Further on in the evidence at the hearings, the legal counsel for the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Dysart, said, and I want the minister to notice this poiht:
The fixing of rates was the prerogative of the government or the parliament of Canada.
The report further states that Chief Commissioner J. A. Cross, K.C., congratulated Mr. Dysart, so that he must have agreed with his remarks.
The Minister of Transport I believe must realize from the evidence submitted that both the legal counsel, Mr. Dysart and the Chief Commissioner Mr. Cross, K.C., were in doubt
Supply-Transport

about their jurisdiction in acting for a subcontractor of the ferries, when they said "they were acting under the Railway Act, possibly supplemented by the Maritime Freight Rates Act." Note those words, Mr. Chairman-"possibly supplemented by the Maritime Freight Rates Act."
It was indeed regrettable that a group of individuals brought this matter up, because they had no authority to speak for the province or to negotiate terms with the subcontractors' board of commissioners for the province.
Without emphasizing those facts any further, it is now up to the Prince Edward Island government, when the board of transport commissioners report after having taken the whole matter under advisement-whoever they are going to report to I do not know-to pay no attention to the report but immediately to take the matter up with the government at Ottawa, parliament and the Minister of Transport, because he and he alone can settle these rates for us and give us justice with regard to the rates.
That is not what the hon. gentleman was saying. He says that the power lies with the government. He is now destroying his own argument.
The power lies with the government and parliament through the Minister of Transport.
Does the hon. gentleman not think we had better await the judgment of the commission before deciding the case?
I am reading from the evidence, just giving the facts.
They have not handed down their judgment yet.
I am quoting what they said to prove that the power was vested in the parliament of Canada.
That is not in the Minister of Transport.

If it is vested in parliament it must come under the cabinet and under some cabinet minister, and the only cabinet minister it could come under is the Minister of Transport.
In closing, I wish to say that I think the minister should take this matter up, and then I am sure he will convince himself, if I am unable to convince him, that parliament and the cabinet and the Minister of Transport have the power, or the Minister of Transport alone has the power to settle this question over which we have so long argued.

I am anxious to enlist the minister's interest in those employees of his who are engaged in a very lonely and, at times, hazardous occupation, namely the lighthouse keepers of our coasts and the personnel who charge the batteries of the different lights. If you are sailing by in a luxury yacht or in a C.P.R. steamer and perhaps wave to the lighthouse keeper's daughter, you are apt to say, "How attractive these red and white buildings look"; but if you land, and I speak as a result of personal visits on the Pacific coast, you will find that conditions in those houses are far from satisfactory. Repairs which, I presume, come under the Department of Public Works, but no doubt would be initiated by the minister's department, are long overdue. There is a story in nearly every case of leaking roofs, inadequate water and cramped conditions, and frequently there is also the story of antiquated equipment. I had occasion to draw to the minister's attention last March an accident which occurred to one of these lighthouse keepers by having to use a hancLstarter for a 20-horsepower stationary diesel engine, and the minister promised at that time that he would look into the matter and see whether automatic starters could be provided for this equipment. Could the minister report now as to whether he is in a position to supply these automatic starters and whether something can be done to improve the lot of these servants of the government?

The position of light-keepers has been enhanced considerably by the department. It is true that lightkeepers live in isolated areas, and the department has been trying to better their position, and has provided for an increase in their allowance. An order in council has been brought down, and a vote is contained in these estimates which will provide a certain amount of money, I think it is $25 a month, to the lightkeeper so as to assist in paying the wages of his assistant. We are doing something, too, with reference to leave, particularly for those who are in isolated spots. To-day practically every keeper on the west coast is getting leave. As regards the matter of more modern equipment to which my hon. friend has referred, I am informed by one of my officers here that the new equipment is actually in the field and should be in the hands of the lightkeepers before long.

I wish to thank the minister for the information that it cost $230,000 to maintain the icebreakers. Can he tell me how much sooner navigation is opened on the St. Lawrence by reason of the operation of the icebreakers? Has he any information about that?

The icebreaker performs a dual purpose. Not only has it to do with the opening of navigation, but it also provides protection from floods to people living on the south shore. Because of the advanced operation of these icebreakers in 1946 we were able to avoid a great deal of flooding on the south side of Montreal. So far as navigation is concerned, were it not for the work of the icebreakers, I believe navigation would open considerably later than it does each year.
Has the minister any figures in regard to time?
It is an average of two to three weeks.
May I ask the minister, in reference to icebreaking in the maritimes, whether a dollar has ever been spent in the last ten years in Halifax harbour?

I wish to endorse wholeheartedly the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo. The lighthouse keepers should be given every consideration. It is true that in many cases they have to live in quarters that are little better than shacks, and when the hon. member from Nanaimo says that the rain beats through the roofs he is correct. That is the case in some lighthouses on the east coast. I would ask the minister to take into consideration the possibility of providing better communication facilities for lighthouses. In one instance I requested the department to provide a telephone, and they replied that it was not in accordance with the policy of the department to provide these facilities in cases such as that in question. In this modern age consideration should be given to a change in .policy, if that is the only reason why telephone service cannot be supplied. Also in particular I would ask the minister whether the construction of the radio beacon at Cross island off Lunenburg harbour has been completed and whether or not an improvement requested for the light at the entrance to Liverpool harbour will be effected in the near future. ,

My hon. friend will
realize that it is difficult to give detailed answers to questions with reference to specific lights, but on the general question of the position of lightkeepers, I may say that it is far better than it has been in the past. This vote contains $40,000 which will be given to lightkeepers and their assistants to improve their position. In the matter of communications, there are no less than 200 radio telephone sets being purchased by the department from War Assets Corporation for installation in these lighthouses. The hon. member has asked two questions having to do with particular lighthouses and I shaH try to get the reply before the committee rises.

I support the request of the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg and the hon. member for Nanaimo. I would point out the necessity of further lighthouse provisions in the county of Cumber-iand, so far as Pugwash is concerned. What provision has been made for the replacement of range lights at Pugwash, destroyed during the w-ar years and not yet restored? There is an emergency light placed there as a range light to guide ships coming into the port of Pugwash. It is one of the best of the out-

ports in the maritime provinces, if not the best. The shipping and lumber interests use the port continuously. It is one of the safest in Canada; but it has been pointed out, both in this house and to the department, that it is necessary to do some dredging in older to take out some of the bends in the channel and also to make it somewhat deeper over the bar at the mouth of the harbour. At the present time ships are able to enter in perfect safety if they have a trained pilot and draw about twenty-one to twenty-two feet. This water can be deepened several feet at a minimum of expense, and the channel leading into the harbour is one of the best natural channels in all Canada. It can be straightened out at the minimum of cost. I realize that this work is not altogether in the minister's department, but by recommendations from him and from his officers I believe the Department of Public "Works would be encouraged to undertake it. I understand that the responsibility for maintaining and rebuilding lighthouses does come under the minister, and I should like to have a statement from him as to what he proposes to do in order to restore this range light at Pugwash, which has been destroyed in the last few years.
I will get the answer.

I wish to speak briefly with reference to lighthouse keepers. The keeper in the town in which I live informed me a short time ago that during 1945 there was a deduction from his salary of, I believe, $15 a month-I will not be sure of the figure-for rent for living in the lighthouse building. That is a condition which has never existed in the past. I do not know where they would expect the lighthouse keeper to live. This man showred me the deduction from his salary, indicating that he had been charged rent for living in the building. That building is on a reef off the mainland about a mile or a mile and a quarter-
From where?

From the town of St. Andrews. It is called New Light or Navy Island bar, I will not say which, in the minister's records. This man's salary is between $1,100 and $1,200 a year. I submit that it is indefensible to charge this man rent for living in such a place, especially in view of the fact that in winter he cannot get ashore. He is there for days at a time when the weather is such that he finds it impossible to go ashore. This deduction has never been made in the past, and I would ask the minister why it was made in 1945.

Would my hon. friend be good enough to give me the details? My officer informs me that there is never any charge for rent. On the contrary, he is generally credited with rent.

Marine serviceill. Steamship inspection and the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines, $255,280.

Last winter representations were made to me by the boat owners of Prince Rupert, particularly the halibut fleet, with respect to the inspection service and the equipment which they must carry when they go to sea. It seems that the inspectors of the department demand on a halibut boat the same life saving equipment as is carried by a full-fledged lifeboat. This is not practical on a halibut boat. What they want is a dory. They should like the inspectors to permit them to carry a dory instead of a boat the size of a lifeboat.
Another thing about which there is a complaint is the three water-tight bulkheads on boats forty-five feet and over. The regulation is expressed in tonnage, but it works out roughly to a boat of that length. When you put in a forward bulkhead you have an airtight compartment and on a wooden boat rot sets in in a remarkably short period of time. They think the department should consult with such responsible people as the boat owners, so that something other than a watertight bulkhead could be put in which would give approximately the same safety measures. They object to this iron-clad rule. I myself have run into it. The result is that small yards, such as Maclean's of Prince Rupert, find it difficult to build boats over forty-five feet because of the demands made on them by the department. I think more consultation should be had with the small shipyards on this type of equipment. Something should be worked out that would be more flexible, so that these men could go ahead with the building of boats. The lifeboat equipment on these boats and the watertight bulkheads are definitely sore points with the halibut men.
I shall be glad to bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the steamship inspection board.

I wish to speak briefly on this matter of steamboat inspection. In January 1946, the Robert Kann was sunk

near Grand Manan island with thirteen persons aboard. At that time there was a lot of criticism around Saint John and Charlotte county of the steamship inspection services. I have nothing to say so far as inspection is concerned; I know nothing about it. But I know the boat that was lost was an old boat in disrepair. There is no question in my mind that it should have been off the route long before that time. At the present time there is a boat there called the Keith Kann, and apparently it is in the same condition as the Robert Kann. I realize that during the war it was difficult to get boats of any kind for this service; but since the war is over and there seems to be plenty of boats available, I think the steamship inspection should be looked after carefully, because the night these thirteen persons perished off that island they left in a lifeboat sixteen feet long and went from the end of Grand Manan island to the Nova Scotia shore. The fact that the boat was only sixteen feet long is a pretty good indication that the craft which sank was in a poor condition. In view of that, I would suggest that they be much more careful in steamship inspection in future for fear the same thing might happen again.

Would the minister give some information supplementary to that given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce respecting plans for the use of the Hudson bay route at Churchill? Would he indicate whether the revenue this year is likely to be increased as a result of shipments of wheat over the Hudson bay route? The information given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not complete; perhaps the Minister of Transport could add to it?

I should not like to add to what was said this morning by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I believe he covered the question fully, namely that the ships at Churchill would take out all the wheat that was there. So far as incoming wheat is concerned, I am afraid I cannot say anything in addition to what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The report is that nine ships will come in and go out of the harbour this summer; and if they do, that will add materially to the revenue of the Hudson Bay railway.

I understand that there is not sufficient wheat available at Churchill. Are arrangements now under way to have additional cargoes of wheat made available, so that wheat may be moved to Europe by the fastest and shortest route during the next few weeks?
I am informed that the season closes before, this year's crop can possibly get there.

There is surely a great deal of wheat available on the prairies. If the government were really concerned about getting wheat to Europe I would suppose that wheat could be supplied. Railway service-
1,15. Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department, $42,000.

How many private cars are used by the Department of Transport? I note that in the details of this item there are four stewards at $1,740 and three porters, at $1,620, making a total of $11,820, exclusive of cost of living bonus. What are these stewards and porters used for?
Then I draw the minister's attention to the item for an official car at $5,000, as set out at page 227 of the estimates. How many cars are used, and what is the purpose of them?

The item provides for five cars, two of which are those of His Excellency the Governor General, and three under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. Of the three, one is assigned to the Prime Minister, one to the Minister of Transport and one is a general, official car for the use of all ministers. The $42,000 compares favourably with amounts spent each year since 1936, when the amount was $57,000, and last year when it was $39,000. This 'has to do with salaries paid to stewards and porters, plus cost of living bonus, in connection with the operation of the three cars I have mentioned, and the two assigned to His Excellency. Then there is the sum of $15,000 for repairs. My hon. friend is probably aware that some of these cars are thirty years old, and it takes substantial repairs to keep them in operation. I might also add that they are not used extensively.
